#4 a kiss

By Dan Waber

EDITORIAL:

“How shared stories connect us” is the name of one lexia in this wandering hypertext novel about falling in love. Written like poetry with elliptical, short phrases, a kiss is the starting point of a biographical rumination on how we come to be the people we are. In the same way that the speaker’s mother “writes down minutiae,” so too the speaker records precise details of memory and in doing so, makes space for the reader to imagine the worlds he conjures, whether they are in his early childhood, “various suburbs outside of Chicago,” or his current terrain in Northern Pennsylvania. Hypertext is well-suited to this novel, which is rewarding no matter which branch you follow, so long as you like slice-of-life stories. The point-of-view is a person who, if he had a million dollars, “wouldn’t change a thing.” The featured image on this webpage is the work’s beautiful story map.

FIN

#6 Writers Are Not Strangers

By Lynda Clark

EDITORIAL:

Writers Are Not Strangers follows Alix, a YouTube videographer and short story writer whose stories the reader can rate on a scale of 1-10. This near-future story, where falling meteors threaten the earth and where Alix’s estranged mother lays dying in a hospital, Alix visits with relatives and evades meteors. The more the reader interacts with this ChoiceScript game, the more the story breaks the “fourth wall” and comments on what it feels like to read other people’s rankings and assessment of one’s writing. This metacritical element puts the reader in the position of both judge and sympathetic reader, commenting on what it means to be a contemporary artist, where quantification of one’s “output” always lurks around the corner, and where one’s worth as an artist is partially determined by such rankings. The reader toggles between offering an assessment of Alix’s writing and navigating through the various paths, which can be roughly classified as “upbeat,” “neutral” or “sad.” How much do the reader’s choices affect the protagonist’s well being? That’s a core question in Writers Are Not Strangers. The short stories, inspired by classic fiction and games (such as Middlemarch and Space Invaders) are very different from the main story of Alix’s life. While Alix is a derivative writer, Writers Are Not Strangers author Lynda Clark breaks new ground with this metacritical story about authoring in the age of social media and quantification.

FIN

#7 Vocable Code (13082018)

By Winnie Soon

EDITORIAL:

Vocable Code is a clever play on code's binary system, and its queer disruptions are both thought provoking and poignant. Playing with code in novel ways, this work foregrounds computer syntaxes and functions, while it also designs a code structure where the code can be spoken/performed. Collecting statements from participants with given constraints, voices are then remixed into a dynamic disarray, creating new sound-image tension and meaning. Vocable Code underscores criticality when designing constraints (which is part of the code writing process). It also features a participatory context for coding that yields a new aesthetic. In this way, the piece reveals processes that might hem us in, as it also points to ways we might break free.

FIN

#8 Jardin de Bots de Brokenenglish.lol

By Canek Zapata

EDITORIAL:

Jardín de bots de brokenenglish [Brokenenglish bot garden] is a family of 16 Twitter bots launched and curated by the Mexican artist Canek Zapata (with Pierre Herrera and David Martínez) addressing disparate topics. Programmed by multiple authors, they act in an entertaining, often comical way. As with any family, they look reasonably good together: they are creative experiments in a specific liminal space, in-between standard and local languages, aiming at lots of laughs. Although they all fall under what Twitter might consider a “proper usage” of bots (generating interesting or creative content), the generated text-image relations are mostly random, hence some of the tweets may be inadvertently polemical. Nonetheless, this family of bots is broad and inclusive: @brokenenglishsi, apparently the Mother Bot, sets the pace for the contradictions ahead: “sí, así, en inglés, una editorial en español [yes, that’s it, in English, an editorial in Spanish]”. These tweets include the Internet slang available across Emojis to Emoticons, Memes and animated GIFs. This is also present in kin bots, although with differing sensibilities. @emojimasemoji adds two Emojis and submits a possible answer for consideration: “🧀📝 + 💲 = 🐙🗿 / El NetArt”; @1botmas1bot is also a “bot de sumas” [addition bot]: “pueblo + biopolítica = siglo xx [people + biopolitics = 20th century]”. @si_o_no_bot (apparently discontinued, or simply on vacation), always replies as “sí o no [yes or no]”, adding an Emoji at the end of each reply; and @un_bot_kawaii – named (ﾉ◕ヮ◕)ﾉ*:･ﾟ✧ - also using emoticons, creating typographic approximations as translations to a universal language: “cuando se sienta a tomar un té [when seating and having tea]/ ( ˘▽˘)っ♨”. @bot_de_colores tweets descriptions of colors: “azul VR; violeta pop art [VR blue; pop art violet]” and @sinestesiabot [“synesthetic bot”] uses figurative language and stylistic devices such as metaphors to define colors: “naranja como el sentir de unos dinosaurios transitando la voz que olvidaste en la fiesta [orange as the feeling of some dinosaurs transiting the voice that you forgot at the party]”; @cristo_elqui, both “bot and prophet,” tweets pretentiously deep reflections about life: “yo soy más hechicero que filósofo/ no resuelvo problemas espectrales/ por desgracia no me equivoco [I am more of a sorcerer than a philosopher/ I don't solve spectral problems/ unfortunately I’m not mistaken]”; @bot_teorico (teoría & so) also ‘imagines’ all sorts of definitions: “El anonimato es una programación reterritorializada. [Anonymity is a reterritorialized programming.]”; and @rolandobartext possibly complements and contextualizes the previous two, ‘simply’ tweeting random quotes/fragments from Spanish translations of three books by the French semiotician Roland Barthes. @feyjonabot is a nearly offensive, hostile personality tweeting twisted love poems: “díselo con flores esta noche a corazón abierto a pensar en mí para vivir por ti [tell it with flowers tonight with an open heart thinking of me to live in your behalf]” and @malumasyntek is also a discomforting bot as heralded in the description: “lo que tú necesitas, baby! [what you need, baby]”. There is however some hedonistic modesty on display: “sé que no soy perfecto pero te diré es que no puede ser lo hermosa que estás [I know I'm not perfect but I'll tell you it can't be how beautiful you are]”. @Li_PoBot tweets longer poems, never original because “cualquier cosa que has escrito ya la escribió un poeta chino del s.IV [whatever you have written has already been written by a 4th century Chinese poet]”; @pegasozorokin is an homage to #ZorokinFest, tweeting fragments of a larger narrative; @PoetaGMadero is a “detective and savage bot,” writing in the form of a diary: “23 de abril/ Sentí que me llamaban de la casa y no me volví. - On February 27 [April 23/ I felt someone calling me from the house and I didn't turn back. - On February 27]”; and @arq_font is a “arquitecto realviceralista [’realvisceralist’ architect]”, tweeting memories of a past that does not exist: “Eso es lo que recuerdo del año 1978. Mi Impala se había ido [That's what I remember from the year of 1978. My Impala was gone]”. Reminding that the past is only a memory and any recollection is subject to distortion and fabrication. Flourishing under the wide umbrella of ergodic forms of expression, not only verbal but also conceptual and symbolic, if you have had enough of bots, bots, and more bots, just glance at the landing page of brokenenglish.lol. A glitched environment embracing what might seemingly be errors such as failures, distortions and visual malfunctions. Used for the purpose of an aesthetical exercise of affirmation, the arguable claim is that countercultural tactics exploit the literary and cultural affiliations of eliterature.

FIN

#9 Poesie Elettroniche

By Fabrizio Venerandi

EDITORIAL:

This interactive EPUB3 is a collection of poetry divided into four parts, each consisting of ten poems. This is the first work in the Italian language to be published in an Electronic Literature Collection. The first section, Occluded Poems, sometimes called “blackout” poetry, reveals words or phrases otherwise blacked out from view when the reader touches or clicks on it. The reader can enlighten the blacked out bars to reveal words or phrases, but the reader will never be able to read the entire poem at once. Touching a new blacked-out block adds an occlusion elsewhere in the poem. This exercise in fragmentation, guesswork, and partial reading tests memory and the reader’s longing for a coherent whole. Temporal Poems, the second section, are poems that bloom at night--“nocturnal jasmine” which “during the day show a verse, and so they end. But at night they unfold, showing during the night other stanzas and other verses,” said author Fabrizio Venerandi. Iridescent poems, section three, permits the reader to find a hidden text by playing with it, touching the words with finger or cursor/ The reader can create new poems by recombining the words, much like “magnetic” or “refrigerator” poetry. Touching poems, section four, allows the reader to create branching poems. “Parent” words, when touched, spawn “child” words that the reader can manipulate—a canny comment on display languages like HTML and CSS where inherited properties govern how words on a webpage look and behave.

FIN

#10 الأدب والفن التفاعلي - Interactive art and literature

By hamza grira#10 الأدب والفن التفاعلي - Interactive art and literature [SHOULD BE RETITLED PRISON CELL Number 06]

EDITORIAL:

Prison Cell Number 06 is an ongoing hypertext novel with a participatory element where readers can contribute ideas, which the author says he will address in future posts. The plot is divided into six parts, accessed through hyperlinks. The link directs you to the novel among other critical and literary works, inside the main interface of the website, including sidebars, news lines, and headlines. Clicking on the novel cover (the white and black image) leads to 14 active links on the right, where the actual narrative starts. It narrates a prisoner's story inside a cell in one of the Arabic countries. Inside his cell, Murad is able to hear different stories from the adjacent market reflecting on the political and economic conditions of the country. Finding important documents belonging to a previous journalist prisoner inside his cell creates a meaning for Murad’s life. These important documents unfold many cases and secrets of political and economic corruption. Murad leaves the prison after a revolution overtakes the country to pursue his mission of revealing the documents' secrets. In this traditional hypertext novel, narration is supported by different images, videos, and audio files. This novel's main characters have actual social media accounts linked to the novel (or did at time of writing). Readers are allowed to participate in developing this novel by emailing their contributions to the author, who aims to add these contributions in an evolving version of the work. [Editorial note: this statement is informed by Dr. Reham Hosny's review of Prison Cell Number 06. Dr. Hosny was an International Consultant to ELC4.]

FIN

#13 How to Rob a Bank

By alan bigelow

EDITORIAL:

How To Rob A Bank is a young Bonnie and Clyde-esque love story about the mishaps that befall a young male bank robber and his female accomplice. This transmedia fiction manifests in the form of animated text conversations between the main characters, and their use of their iPhones to Google search, text, game, and use other apps on the phone as part of their capers. The story is an immersive experience generated through readers’ hands-on use of apps, maps, imagery, animations and audio. Bigelow’s award winning 2016 multimodal work foregrounds how social technology has become a core element of daily life, and helps us see the way that social technologies structure lived experience. The mirror effect of the character/reader’s use of personal devices as they read this piece makes this narrative relatable, shining light on widespread digital traversing behaviors. And yet, the storytelling is also traditional in its linear development with five sequential episodes.

FIN

#16 Please, don’t touch me!

By Beat Suter

EDITORIAL:

Please, don’t touch me! is an artgame about asymmetric control wherein the player (the "master") exerts absolute authority over the avatar. In other words, the player is gifted a “fun slave” to manipulate. Adopting a retro game aesthetic, it is a game that reflects on digital cultural issues as it weaves integrated/artificial audio with the spoken human word. This clever and playful work highlights the dilemma of bullying in social media and video games, as it references oft-quoted statements from well-known adventure games. It is at once a silly game, but also an uncanny meditation on power, control, and harm. In its own unique way, it points ironically towards the ways in which our analog world can actually be like the artificial digital worlds we create.

FIN

#22 Piksel Zdrój

By Olaf Keller

EDITORIAL:

Piksel Zdrój is a collaborative hypertext novel consisting of 16 separate sections, developed by groups of authors recruited through a literary workshop led by Mariusz Pisarski. Pixel Zdrój consists of 16 separate stories divided into 250 segments connected by over 1300 URLs, of which about 600 are rhetorical links, a kind of metacommentary. Each author offers a distinctive writing style in their micro-storyworld, contributing to a plot revolving around an unsolved crime. It is the best Polish collaborative hypertext novel to date, captivating with its storyline set at a seashore resort during the summer, and intelligent use of hypertextual structure. Human and algorithmic interaction and expressive algorithms are employed mostly through clicking the hypertextual links, although a more linear form of reading is possible when following plots created by specific co-authors. Piksel Zdrój nicely combines a fixed structural scheme of the linear narratives with ergodic, branched reading enabled by the way its lexias are linked. The whole work is illustrated with 200 illustrations, photos, audio and video files. [Editorial note: this statement is informed by Dr. Anna Nacher's review of Piksel Zdrój. Dr. Nacher was an International Consultant to ELC4.]

FIN

#37 Generation Loss (after Alvin Lucier)

By Pascalle Burton

EDITORIAL:

Generation Loss (after Alvin Lucier) is a response to Alvin Lucier’s 1969 work I am sitting in a room, in which the artist’s speech is recorded, played back and recorded again until the iterations become unrecognizable and incorporate the frequencies of the physical space. Generation Loss contemplates duplication and decay; the “generations” responding to concepts of text degeneration in a digital environment and acknowledging the material conditions of Lucier’s conceptual approach to experimental music. The literary dimension is to find the signal in the noise. Human reception of sound interprets its meaning, how it reflects on the human condition, even in sound that follows the strict ordering of physical rules of decay.

FIN

#38 TEXTUAL AUTOMATA

By Joel Swanson

EDITORIAL:

Textual Automata is a beautiful play on words, and it reads like a generative crossword puzzle of magical connections in language and meaning. Transposing the concept of cellular reproduction onto how language lives and dies, the work is built upon the concept of the British mathematician John Conway's Game of Life from 1970. In Conway’s work, simple code-based rules are used to govern cellular automata. In Textual Automata simple code-based rules are applied to a linguistic context. Input a word into the stark black grid, and the resulting generativity evolves from a list of synonyms. If a synonym for a chosen word can be found in the thesaurus, the textual automata will grow and branch associated meanings. You can input words into the grid as it grows, shifting language output in new directions. As a form of algorithmic concrete poetry, this project points to how structural linguistics can serve as a basis for developing form, pattern, and complexity. Truly a work that combines interactivity, language, and human-machine co-creation, this piece is a wonderful example of how elit can also be conceptual art. The literary experience is reinforced by our impulse to read meaning into the associations generated by the synonyms.

FIN

#44 The Buoy

By Meredith Morran

EDITORIAL:

It’s unusual to see an author use PowerPoint expressively because this software is almost exclusively used as a work productivity tool. That’s why The Buoy, Meredith Morran’s poetic auto-fiction, delights with its surprising use of diagrams and visual metaphors of sailboat racing to talk about growing up queer in Texas, a socially conservative state. It is also about the limits of language to bring identity into a knowable experience. In a world where infographics, diagrams, and quantitative representations of human experience are increasingly relied upon to explain the messiness of human experience, Morran’s formal progression of related diagrams undoes the apparent simplicity of those illustrations. Specifically, the piece employs tactical concepts in sailboat racing, terminology presented by cultural theorist, Eve Sedgwick in her text Touching Feeling, and larger theories surrounding semiotics and language as The Buoy strives to provide answers to questions such as: How do we talk about things that are hard to understand? How do we talk about ourselves? How do we talk to others? Technically simple, this piece demonstrates how even productivity apps can be sites of rich autobiographical disclosure and rumination.

FIN

#47 Millón y una noches

By Pablo Sanguinetti

EDITORIAL:

Millón y una noches [A Million and One Nights] is a Twitter bot that generates and posts a short story in Spanish every day, “al menos hasta la próxima noche [at least until the next night].” Borrowing its title from The Arabian Nights, a folk tales collection compiled in Arabic and also known as The Thousand and One Nights, this bot demonstrates how eliterature reflects the human spirit through diversity, intertwining different ages, cultures, languages and platforms. In addition, it is able to preserve and translate emblematic literary techniques and motifs into digital content, while experimenting with narratology through non-human storytelling and creative practices. In The Arabian Nights, Scheherazade, female character and storyteller, tells the monarch Shahryar endless tales to entice his curiosity and postpone her execution. Also eluding death, the life expectancy of this bot is of at least one more night, always the following one, hence (virtually) endlessly reflecting the fragmentary, collaborative nature of the tales. These simple yet compelling short tales gather stories within stories, encoding the ‘embedded narrative’ technique as an algorithmic procedure. Mythical in content, these digitales are about adventures involving heroes and knights, witches and ghosts, dreams and nightmares, as their Arabian ancestors, varying from love stories to short tragedies, ironic poems to narrative travesties. Created with Cheap Bots, Done Quick! and written in Tracery, the Python source code is available online, allowing readers-authors to modify the original structure and lexicon.

FIN

#48 "beauty routine", from The Offline Website Project

By Alex Saum

EDITORIAL:

To experience “Beauty Routine” and other installations of The Offline Website Project, you would have to get directions from map software to Alex Saum’s home in Berkeley, California and pay a visit, because the project runs locally on her own machine. As with some other conceptual elit, where the idea is more invigorating than the experience of interacting with it, The Offline Website Project is a dematerialized networked communication totally localized to Saum’s home. While a fresh idea, the concept isn't bold or exciting enough to sustain one through the dullness of watching Saum brush her teeth, wash her face and apply makeup. These activities take center stage in her brave performance. Saum unmasks the illusion of effortless, “natural” beauty in the specific medial context (YouTube) where makeup tutorials, streaming Influencer hijinks, and the direct-address vlogging style are common, and profitable for Alphabet which owns YouTube. Saum deconstructs the tropes and conventions of makeup tutorials. Her refusal to host these vlogs on the web draws attention to technical infrastructures that profit from the confected intimacy of watching people in their bedrooms and bathrooms. “Beauty Routine” is thus a feminist infrastructural critique. Collecting the work here in ELC4, we denature it by making it available to you on demand, undoing the conceptual heft of Saum’s refusal for the larger purpose of documentary accessibility.

FIN

#52 Emblem/as

By Tina Escaja (Alm@ Pérez)

EDITORIAL:

Emblem/as uses flags, banners and spoken word as compressions of human identity and cultural belonging. Gesturing to the sounds of English, Spanish, Catalan and Spanglish as overlapping spaces, the author gives readers a haptic experience of place-making as the reader’s cursor glides over the flags, triggering keywords spoken by the author in English, Spanish and Spanglish. Anagrams point to notions of anxiety, division and pain (Ansiado, Dissent, Duelo, SOS), as well as longing (Deseado). Other meanings address issues of imperialism and informatic control (data) as well as perpetual tensions: Todo/Nada;U-No;O-Dios(All/Nothing; One/No; God/Hate).

FIN

#54 When Rivers Were Trails

By Elizabeth LaPensee

EDITORIAL:

Featuring over thirty Indigenous contributors, When Rivers Were Trails is an interactive adventure game which recreates the experience of displacement from traditional territory. As an Anishinaabeg in the 1890s, the player is forced from their traditional territory in Minnesota, and migrates west to California to claim unseen (and unvaluable) tribal land conferred by the Dawes Allotment Act. Unlocking historical and traditional stories during the game, the player will face Indian Agents, civilians appointed by the President of the United States to serve as an ambassador to Native American nations living in the region. Agents were responsible for being the eyes, ears, and mouth of the U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs to Native communities. The player will also meet people from different nations, hunt, fish, and canoe as they attempt to balance their wellbeing during displacement. This work is significant due to its educational materials and sheer wealth of perspectives, stories, and languages. As a counter narrative to the 1971 classic adventure game Oregon Trail, When Rivers Were Trails emphasizes sharing and spiritual wellness over a game mechanic driven by acquisition of food and money.

FIN

#55 The Gathering Cloud

By J. R. Carpenter

EDITORIAL:

The Gathering Cloud is a hybrid print and web-based work which addresses the environmental impact of seemingly effervescent “cloud” storage by calling attention to the materiality of the clouds in the sky and on server farms. Both are commonly perceived to be infinite resources, at once vast and immaterial; both, decidedly, are not. The Gathering Cloud’s collage of found objects on the theme of weather and cloud computing integrates fragments from Howard’s “On the Modifications of Clouds” (1803), contemporary media and environmental theory, and animated gifs made from images appropriated from cloud storage services. The ominous “gathering” cloud alludes to climate disaster fed by our ravenous appetite for cloud computing services: ecommerce, social media, virtual work, blockchain. There's also a print iteration of The Gathering Cloud, a paper book lovingly “shared through gift, trade, and mail art economies.” This printed version is post-digital: small-batch, artisanal printing, hand-packaged to travel slowly via mail. Carpenter’s online/printed book combination invites us to reckon with tradeoffs: “always-on” networked connectivity that ransacks calm weather; instant gratification juxtaposed against waiting for something to arrive, eventually, by mail.

FIN

#57 Everything is going to be OK

By Nathalie Lawhead

EDITORIAL:

Everything is going to be OK is a chaotic ride through a rabbithole in what Katie Schaag calls a “queer femme internet aesthetic”, full of bright shades and hyperanimated movement. Its neon colors and jittering layout are nostalgic call-outs to 1990s DIY internet, the glitter of geospaces and online ’zines melding with the kawaii culture of Hello Kitty and other East Asian anime and visual novels. The adorable bunny avatars and cutesy blobby characters who hop through various games and scenarios, however, are brittle-bright window dressing for the dark underlay of the everyday struggle with dread and depression. The work offers glimpses into its soul through layers of surreal humor, occasionally revealing the profound inner battle to come to terms with trauma. The execution is flawless, as the ’zine presents dozens of different mini-works for exploration, interaction, and reflection; though the artist describes it as “broken,” nothing about this work is a misstep. It engenders feelings of hysterical laughter devolving to sobs, setting the reader/player on a roller coaster of adorable gore and hypercolor lucid dreams. As such, it can be an ideal text for teaching the power of interactive storytelling for emotional effect, and to bring Gen Z into elit, though content warnings for mentions of depression, self-harm, and suicidal thoughts should be included.

FIN

#62 The Data Souls

By David Thomas Henry Wright

EDITORIAL:

“There is no doubt the Informatic Age populations revered data.” So begins this dystopic, futurist “archeological” find of seven rusted data storage drives from our present day, called “the Early Informatic Age (2000-2100 CE).” The surviving data sets seem not to be mutually-informing or even coherent (currency values from 2011–2019, the Human Freedom Index, provincial Chinese male/female birth ratios, Australian rabbit populations, global temperature anomalies, and national average time spent on the Internet per day). Scientists in the future debate the significance of these surviving data sets from long ago. This work uses those found datasets to populate generated poetry. Triggered by clicking avatars of ancient Egyptian gods, snippets of data write and rewrite before the reader’s eyes. An exercise in conceptual writing, The Data Souls prompts consideration of our reverence for quantified data, and penchant for measuring even things that seem inimical to quantification such as spirituality and social well-being. Its futurist setting creates the illusion of historical distance by making all the story pages accessible through avatars from ancient Egypt, suggesting that the found data storage is as distant from the story’s present day as our world today is from ancient Egypt. Ambient sounds relevant to each “story” can be activated by tapping a discreet media player in the upper-right of any webpage.

FIN

#63 Not_A_Number (NAN)

By Xavier Leton and others

EDITORIAL:

Not_A_Number is a collection of 10 place-based/site-specific creations resulting from multiple collaborations (in the works featured in ELC4, Leton with Balpe, Bachman, Lemoine and Capponi), selected from the project Les VillesAllantVers. The concept behind these animated text-image literary works is apparently straightforward: the appropriation of found media from public spaces and transports, repurposing them into video poetry. These recirculate in installations and performances as well as in “inappropriate networks” such as Facebook or Linkedin. Adopted tactics include the “hijacking” of 360° video footage,” encircling animated sentences in the video frame and producing a “fly on the wall” effect. N_A_N widens our understanding of street art, incorporating performative and material aspects from post-digital aesthetics, blurring the boundaries between real and virtual, analog and digital. Concerned with politics and power, engaged in activism and involvement, these Situationist strategies further promote a critical discussion of the current digital environment as a common place/non-place, encouraging the reader to perceive the digital arena as human – “not a number” – a shared territory for resistance, “by the people and for the people.”

FIN

#66 Déprise / Loss of Grasp

By Serge Bouchardon

EDITORIAL:

It is hard to overstate the impact of Déprise/Loss of Grasp. Told in six vignettes from the point-of-view of a man “losing his grasp” on his marriage, his relationship with his son, and even his recognition of himself in the mirror, Déprise develops its themes in stunningly original human/computer interactions. Each touch interaction the reader has with the story interface (typing keys, touching a mousepad or screen, clicking) advances the plot and deepens the reader’s emotional connection with the baffled protagonist. The machine’s camera, audio, touchpad (or touchscreen) and keyboard create playable experiences that dramatize the narrator’s eroding confidence. The reader is invited, for example, to swipe up or down to transform the same words into a love letter or break up note while Edith Piaf croons in the background. In January 2020, the Arabic, Chinese, German, Hungarian and Polish versions of Déprise were published online. “Every translation required changes to the original version in French but also to the other versions,” observes primary author Serge Bouchardon. This makes Déprise not just an internationally accessible work, but also an internationally re-created one: translations influenced Bouchardon’s new, 2019 adaptation of the original to let it run on mobile devices. Déprise/ Loss of Grasp is the first work of digital literature to make voices, animations and interactivity accessible in ten languages. But don’t let this work’s groundbreaking importance make you approach the work reverently. On the contrary, Déprise is best approached playfully, savoring how touching the computer influences story development.

FIN

#69 Ringing the Changes and its online companion Liberty Ring!

By Stephanie Strickland

EDITORIAL:

Stephanie Strickland, a founder of the eliterature community, has long explored the tension and complementarity between textuality and human/computer interaction. Ringing the Changes is a printed book of outputs from code she wrote to emulate the precision of chime sequences in ancient bell towers. Using code to shrink the distance between our own moment and bellringers—who, in the seventeenth century, memorized long, mathematically precise sequences and rang the huge bells for the entire village to hear—Strickland explores how code can be a kind of time travel and thought experiment. The printed output of Ringing the Changes is not inconsequential, but the main show is the code that creates sonorous chiming output: read aloud these words extracted and combined from 23 different texts and let your breath be an Aeolian harp. Strickland uses the metaphor of chiming as a metacommentary on the poetic act, and aligns herself with the poets through the ages who made music and meaning with the materials at hand. The online companion Liberty Ring! gives a taste of the interactivity between the code and the printed output, which Strickland shaped into the interactive format of a printed poetry collection. Much as the gravitational constraints of bell shape, weight, distance from the ground and momentum would produce a unique peal high off the ground in a tower, so too the particular contexts and histories of the source texts Strickland uses impart a rich range of tones. Play the interactive site, or see the book’s generously annotated GitHub repository to try your own hand at ringing the ancient, hefty bells remediated into code and poetic words.

FIN

#70 The Winnipeg: The Poem that Crossed the Atlantic

By María Mencía

EDITORIAL:

Winnipeg: The Poem That Crossed the Atlantic is both a personal story and a war story about migration. The author’s grandfather, a Spanish Civil War refugee imprisoned in a French concentration camp, was rescued by Chilean poet Pablo Neruda, whose diplomatic mission successfully liberated 2350 prisoners of war by relocating them to Valparaiso, Chile on the cargo ship The Winnipeg in 1939. Both a community poem and a research project, The Poem that Crossed the Atlantic is a sea of animated words fed by posts made by refugee family members and researchers. To read the poem is to plunge into an ocean of infinite canvas where animated letters, on hover, highlight into words culled from the project’s archival documents in Spanish, French and English. The experience of reading these fleeting words is fragmentary and non-sequential. The more time a reader spends interacting, the more a storyline begins to emerge. The initial disorientation--where am I? Where am I being taken by this poem?--mimics the disorientation felt by war refugees plucked from prison and transported on The Winnipeg. Readers who prefer a more ordered experience may consult the project’s Archive tab, which presents all of the poem’s source texts. Winnipeg: The Poem That Crossed the Atlantic is a multilingual, community-based project of memory, migration, and translation. “The critics may erase all of my poetry,” wrote Neruda about transporting refugees to Chile, “but this poem that I today remember, nobody will be able to erase.”

FIN

#73 Scriptpoemas

By Antero de Alda

EDITORIAL:

These 75 “Scriptpoems” programmed by Antero de Alda between 2005 and 2018 (the year of his death) use scripting languages to interrogate the character and function of poetry in the digital age. They all operate under one very simple constraint: to code the word “poem” so that it can endure a diverse set of operations and transformations, in form and substance, at the level of expression and content. As a result, these poems are calligrammatic and nonetheless their visual arrangement is inconstant, since it is not bound by the static page format. As such, the ‘illegible poem’ cannot be read; the ‘hidden poem’ must be discovered; the ‘Google poem’ can only be deciphered with effort, scattered as it is inside a shredded map; etc. Alda was a concrete and visual poet, publishing his poetry mostly in magazines and books. Also, he was a photographer and a teacher, an profusion of arts that is apparent in this repertoire of short and sharp kinetic ideograms, employing ‘concrete’ digital strategies to ironically address representations of cyberculture. Displaying an acute understanding of semiotic experimentalism and iconography, Alda’s production also stems from his previous experiments with computer-generated and computer-animated poetry, namely his BASIC poems from 1986 (recently “discovered,” reprinted and emulated), and the Flash poems that are currently obsolete.

#74 Quarto do Esquecimento

By Vinícius Rutes Henning

EDITORIAL:

Quarto do Esquecimento is a re-reading and remediation of the book Quarto de Despejo: Diário de uma Favelada (translation: Eviction Room: Diary of a Female Slum-Dweller) written by Carolina Maria de Jesus in São Paulo, Brazil. While this elit remediation of Jesus’s memoir is simple at the level of interface, its simplicity makes an important point about the source text and the limited options available to its author, who published her diary August 1960. Vinícius Rutes Henning transposes the printed diary to this digital remediation, using a Unity game engine to simulate the illusion of choice. Each day the reader is forced to choose between two actions, and then a fragment of the original diary appears. As time goes by, it becomes apparent the limitation and frustration of Carolina's few choices. This effect is further enhanced with the use of songs composed by Jesus that are little known, and recent photos of Rio de Janeiro's favelas. By bringing this book to the digital medium, we editors hope to bring it to new readers: time spent in the “Forgetfulness Room.”

#75 novelling

By Will Luers, Hazel Smith and Roger Dean

EDITORIAL:

Remix was a feature of early novels in the mid-eighteenth century, such as Tristram Shandy which inspired readers to make fake continuations, songs, pornographic parodies, and the like. In novelling, the authors materialize this tradition with tools and palettes of our own time, remixing tropes of literature, music and cinema. Novelling questions the novel's basis in plot, character and words, continuing the experiments of Woolf and Joyce by carrying modernism through pastiche and remix into questions about how reading/playing interactive art as four characters immersed in their isolated life-worlds can be transported elsewhere by what they are reading. Novelling allows the reader to traverse an intimate space between interior monologue and plot, a kind of technical free indirect discourse abetted by Luers’ variable and deterministic system of selection and arrangement. In the tradition of the OuLiPo, novelling presents the reader with novelistic potential that one’s own traversal realizes.

FIN

#79 Bucle: archivo de ficciones

By Vinicius Marquet

EDITORIAL:

“Ulises Carrión is not dead,” declares author Vinicius Marquet, “and maybe he has never been.” Bucle: Archivo de ficciones (translation: Loop: An Archive of Fictions) is inspired by Carrión’s play with the book as a material object with particular inspiration from his famous manifesto "The New Art of Making Books" (1975). Taking the challenge from Carrión, Marquet explores the force and limits of the PDF, a format intended to support a stable reading experience across digital environments. Marquet makes the PDF interactive with internal links, videos and embedded sounds. His PDF “book” is beautifully designed, and uses the PDF medium in a way that pushes against the software’s intended function. What would Carrión make of the PDFs goal of stability and reader passivity? From the first moment of engaging Bucle in the Adobe PDF Reader, one is confronted with choices. The PDF “takes over” your full screen, triggering a pop-up warning from Adobe. “The characters are not what they say they are,” says a voice in English. A hypertext fiction based on real life events that happened to the author during his research about Ulises Carrión's life and legacy, the story adds alternative biographical events based on interviews with friends, ultimately asking: to what extent is an archive an artwork?

FIN

#80 Aphiddd

By Andy Campbell

EDITORIAL:

In the way one lifts a rock off the damp ground to reveal skittering insects, Aphidd rewards interaction. The reader navigates this browser-based 3D poem, toggling via the computer touchpad to explore a rotting tree that is host to aphids sucking the nutrients from the tree. Ambient sound of insects emplaces the reader in this fecund, dark landscape. Insect volume increases the closer one zooms into the words, which seem to be spoken from the point-of-view of an aphid, whose addition to two extra “D”s in every word that requires only one D is a clever sound pun on the volumetric dimensions of this 3D poem. The sound pun also suggests that the speaker is nonhuman, an insect in a rotting piece of plant matter. Words stream over the natural objects as colonies of ants or aphids might. The poem is an organism whose consciousness raises awareness of how decay feeds life. In a digital environment of precariously short elit lifespans, where literary works quickly decay and stop working when the software or operating system is no longer “supported,” the message of Aphiddd has an especial irony: “How well you look / a glittering winddd / all the life you’ve taken from me / your presence shines/ suspendeddd by mirrors / but I grow back.”

FIN

#85 Living Will

By Mark C. Marino

EDITORIAL:

Living Will is a serious story about colonialism written in a jocular, nineteenth-century first-person voice. At its heart is a paternity scandal involving our unreliable narrator, E.R. Millhouse, whose systemic exploitation of people and natural resources in the Democratic Republic of Congo to enrich himself–and now, his heirs–is a microcosm of the shattering effects of resource extraction as an Original Sin. Set in present-day, the dying Millhouse sets his four heirs in competition with each other to claim the most inheritance; the reader can choose to play as any one of the heirs. A game mechanic pipes in the actual trading pricing of coltan, an element essential to cell phones and other computers and the foundation of Millhouse’s ill-gotten fortune, to calculate the worth of Millhouse’s estate. The most interesting and innovative thing about Living Will is the secret paternity scandal that unfolds in the Living Will’s source code (find it by clicking on the "tutorial.js" file). In it, readers are given clues to deduce Millhouse’s sexual exploits and the heavy legacy they leave behind. Whether you do speedruns of this game or savor the story’s Victorian allusions and quirky jokes, Living Will succeeds via a poetics of frustration. The game doesn’t resolve neatly, and can seem “broken.” The frustration one feels trying to amass inheritance is procedural rhetoric: as the reader plays, frustration with the game’s broken qualities offers a commentary on the jagged relationships and wreckage wrought by colonial greed that pits all the characters against each other.

#94 Letters to X . vol/1

By Jessica Barness

EDITORIAL:

Part Mad-Lib, part homage to Christopher Strachey’s M.U.C. Love Letter Generator (1952—arguably the first work of digital literature), Letters to X amplifies the possibilities of “handwritten” love notes by allowing the reader to move panes around and either enter one’s own Mad-Lib like entries, or read a letter X has received with some of the personalization redacted. There’s a palimpsestic quality to the layers of personal notes; more conceptually interesting than emotionally affecting, this work invites reader performance as a way to think critically about the effortless ease of “social” media.

#95 Compasses

By Allison Parrish

EDITORIAL:

The monochromatic aesthetic of the digital zine Compasses complements the spare poems generated by a machine learning model with two parts: a "speller" and a "sounder-out" (see author’s description for how these work). Designed to output in the shape of a compass rose, this new form of generative concrete poetry reveals intriguing word relationships and its governing metaphor, the compass rose, suggests wayfinding. Which way does the wind blow? is the question a compass rose was originally designed to measure. In Parrish’s version, we can imagine various scenarios suggested by the poems, such as: how does spatial proximity incline us to see connections between things? What work is done by the spaces in-between? Whether the poem’s subject is southwestern U.S. states, a baseball diamond, the four Hogwarts houses, or many other scenarios, these poems give us the literary apparatus to think about how slight variations in letter combinations from the four points of a machine-made “compass” unleash the imagination to play with adjacency, and invite us to think about how proximity tricks the brain into mapping contextual connections.

#97 Waveform

By Richard A Carter

EDITORIAL:

Where does the shore begin and the sea end? Waveform, an eco-poem, uses drone footage of shorelines to generate stanzas about the Anthropocene. It is difficult to distinguish the threshold between wave and shore. Carter transposes the data gathered from drones and machine vision of the sea/shore into various material contexts (a film; stills in a book; projections in an installation). This site-specific work invites us to think and feel climate change prompted by sense perceptions and the ruminations that Waveform prompts us to consider. The technology that makes this work possible is not a neutral observer. Like the natural seascapes they quantify, digital sensors, drones and computational processing systems are in dialogue with their environments and the humans who program them, capturing a new way to view the volatile environment adapting to radical warming.

#105 Arborescencia Programada

By Enrique García Alcalá

EDITORIAL:

Arborescencia Programada [Programmed Arborescence] creates a visual representation of a tree as users type words on their keyboard. The initial blank screen is the surface of interaction. The algorithm identifies some of the words in a database (based on writings by di Giorgio, Oliver, Hughes, Watanabe and Rilke), and the written words are displayed in connection with the matched words. Subsequently, the text grows as branches and ramifications. This artwork offers a metaphor to define electronic writing and literature. Simultaneously, it demonstrates how the internet, language, and communication work. Based on trees and branches, it revives Deleuze and Guattari's concept of rhizome (in Mille Plateaux) and the construction of a philosophical notion of network with interchangeable elements and without a center. This notion remains plausible when considering the inherent variability of electronic textuality. In fact, this digital work may seem contradictory since it elaborates on the idea of ​​a tree-book, or ‘image of the world’, which Deleuze and Guattari oppose to the rhizome-text. However, the hierarchical logic of the book opposes the random forms of branches produced by the generator. These expand along multiple directional axes without ever settling for a definite point. Furthermore, these arboreal poems mimicking fractal structures use Markov Chains to produce disparate possible sentences in response to the text written by the user. These programmed trees of intertwined texts demonstrate that under the rule of numerical representation, every text develops as a rhizome, in a simulation where mediation is replaced by perpetual remediation and all is encapsulated in the digital medium.

FIN

#109 brokenenglish.lol

By María Cristina Hall; Silvia Castelán; Mónica Nepote; Camila Gb

EDITORIAL:

BrokenEnglish.lol is a large compendium of net poetry by mostly GenZ and millennial Latin American poets founded in 2016. Its title mocks the presumed centrality of English to cultural production and asserts the value of under-age-40 new media artists working in Spanish, not “broken English.” For ELC4, co-founder Canek Zapata curated four works as a distillation of the larger site. ELC4 editors thank Zapata and the new media curator Doreen Rios, both of Mexico City, who recommended the four artists featured in this entry: Silvia Castlán (🌹🌹🌹), Maria Cristina Hall (Cuando me di cuenta que no era white), Mónica Nepote (Lengua Parasita), and Camila Gb (Für Cecilio).

Castlán’s 🌹🌹🌹poem takes as its starting point a cryptic Instagram post made by Britney Spears: was Spears indicating her endorsement of the Democratic Socialists of America? Using the vernacular of Instagram–emojis, gifs, collaged images, sound loops–Castlán’s poem cannily reflects on sexism.

Maria Cristina Hall’s Cuando me di cuenta que no era white (“When I Realized I Wasn’t White”) uses a very simple background color shift (flashing black and white) to indicate the ambiguity of her racial status, which the poem examines in various scenarios where the author’s racial status is remarked upon by others, and how the author feels about it.

Mónica Nepote investigates the “parasitic tongue” by writing recombinant phrases in discrete sections of Spanish and English, but the recombinant verse is not evident on first glance because the landing page is flat and unyielding. It’s only by hunting through the code that one finds a link to the generative work. The words are layered on top of a video of cell mitosis and a haunting ambient soundtrack.

Camila Gb wrote Für Cecilio to commemorate the death of a guppy fish that she shared with a lover who broke her heart. Like Castlán, she uses the vernacular of emojis and gifs to reframe the underwater garden of desire as a place of “toothless words” and otherworldly sea creatures.

#110 Bad News

By Ben Samuel, Adam Summerville

EDITORIAL:

Bad News is a roleplay game set as an installation that combines artificial intelligence and live improvisational acting. It’s a one-on-one experience where the player engages an actor whose improvised narrative pathways are summoned through livecoding and AI. The setting: it’s the summer of 1979. A resident in a computer-generated American small town has died alone at home, and a mortician's assistant—the in-person player standing in front of the Bad News installation booth—is tasked with tracking down and notifying the next of kin. The first action in this RPG is for the player to meet the mortician, played by a live actor in the booth. After receiving instructions from the mortician, the player navigates the computer-generated town on a tablet, interacting with its residents, who are each played live by the actor. Throughout gameplay, an unseen wizard (a livecoding programmer behind the booth’s curtain) eavesdrops on the player and actor to manage the unfolding experience. 140 years of the town’s history is simulated, which provides a rich source of narrative pathways the programmer can activate through code. Through its unique blend of human and machine performance, Bad News meditates on the trauma of losing a life and, ultimately, how machines today facilitate our intimate communities, which was not true in 1979. Bad News was performed several hundred times in the United States, Canada, and Italy, including at the Slamdance Film Festival, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and IndieCade, where it won the 2016 Audience Choice award.

#111 forgotten nights

By Peter Hebden

EDITORIAL:

When we look to the sky to seek patterns among the stars–looking for shapes that remind us of a bear, an archer, a dipping spoon–we are surrendering to the idea that we seek larger meaning for our lives by finding patterns in nature that might reveal clues. Forgotten nights taps into this longing by allowing the reader to reveal stars by clicking on a seemingly empty night sky. Each click loads a line of poetry spoken by a male voice. The reader/listener changes the lines by adding or removing stars, and with it, the journey of moving through the poem. Unusual, elegant and beautifully coherent, forgotten nights transports the reader to an experience of randomness, imbuing the auditory experience with a search for meaning akin to what people have done for millennia as they gaze at the moon in the night sky. Literary readers interested to pursue intertextual connections may wish to consult Stephanie Strickland’s elit-and-printed poetry collection V, which Hebden acknowledges as an influence. (See also here in ELC4 a more recent work of Strickland’s, Ringing the Changes/Liberty Ring.)

#125 醉詠詩 Zui Yong Shi

By 楊仁（Ren Yang)

EDITORIAL:

Emulating the ancient Tang Dynasty poet Li Po (circa 8th century), student Ren Yang generates Chinese WuYan JueJu poetry. Combined with the melody and flow, people can actually sing the generated poetry, since all of the words are carefully selected to create simple, evocative poetic lines. To read the poem, begin at the top right column and move down. The poem’s pentatonic tones will play on their own, and you sing the words in Chinese (or in the English translations provided on hover). Li Po’s poetry is known for its clear imagery and conversational tone, notes the Poetry Foundation entry about Li Po who influenced 20th-century American poets such as Ezra Pound and James Wright. In Ren Yang’s generated remediation of Li Po’s poem, singing 醉詠詩 keeps with the theme established in the original about “singing intoxicatingly” (“醉詠詩”). An exhortation to seize the joys of the present moment, Li Po’s《春夜宴桃李園序》inspires Ren Yang to explore how Po’s ancient pastoral sheds light on our current moment of multitasking and attention scarcity. While the pastoral has always been a romantic ideal dreamed up by unfulfilled urbanites, in Yang’s poem the simplicity of poetic lines and the simple pentatonic music perform the poem’s argument: live simply in good company. Try singing along yourself!

FIN

#126 Big Data

By Diego Bonilla

EDITORIAL:

Big Data is a generative YouTube poem that runs via an algorithm, so that verses are scrambled to generate infinite combinatorial compositions. Addressing the rights of privacy and personal data on the web, it is a seemingly infinite remix on demand. The randomized sequencing of lexia is performed by diverse readers, regenerating itself differently each time it is executed. The interactive poem points to the vast collection of personal information that is culled online and purposed in ways invisible to the online participant. In each regeneration, appropriate grammatical and semantic structures are achieved. Massive collection of personal data and subsequent statistical processing, the poem suggests, is leading us to a bleak reality. It emphasizes how inferential behavioral statistics achieve persuasive goals of unseen actors: the reader is acted upon. And yet, this work runs on the very data and statistical processes it is critiquing, suggesting the banality of post-digital life, where even critique relies upon the systems that make it and deliver it to an audience.

FIN

#132 PEACEFUL DREAM

By Ottar Ormstad

EDITORIAL:

peaceful dream is a Chinese version of Ottar Ormstad's first book, het still, a variation on the Norwegian word for “silence,” stillhet. In each corner on every second page in het still, there is one word in Norwegian, Ormstad’s native language. However, the four words do not constitute a sentence. This version in Chinese is not an attempt to translate the original work. Instead, “for design reasons,” notes Ormstad, “I selected signs that gave kind of the same mood as the original Norwegian.” Ormstad's printed book requires active engagement. The placement of the words on the page forces the reader to use hands, eyes and cognition to make meaning of the work. The basic idea behind the film is the same. By selecting Chinese ideographs in combination with pictures, videos and music, Ormstad creates a feeling of a peaceful dream that requires active eye movement and cognitive decoding. The words are connected to nature and feelings. The second part includes Chinese versions of what Ormstad calls "lettercarpets," which he has created in all his films.

#134 The Infinite Woman

By Katie Schaag

EDITORIAL:

The Infinite Woman remixes excerpts from two mid-20th century books, Edison Marshall’s novel The Infinite Woman (1950) and Simone de Beauvoir’s The Second Sex (1949). Marshall’s novel is a melodramatic, male-authored, first-person fictional narrative in the voice of Lola, who embodies the ideal of “natural” womanhood. Beauvoir’s existential interrogation of the unnaturalness of gender roles deconstructs the myth of “the eternal feminine.” The Infinite Woman web app literalizes the concept of gendered infinitude by outputting lines that will endlessly generate combinations or erasures of the two source texts, creating a process in code and in the reading experience that performs the critique underpinning both the source texts. Conceptually, Schaag’s work interrogates the limits of gender as a performative category. Meanwhile, fog slowly erases the screen, materializing “the misty mirror of the eternal feminine,” an evocative image from Marshall and Beauvoir.

FIN

#135 SONAR

By Daniela Côrtes Maduro

EDITORIAL:

Originally created to be experienced in the context of an art installation, SONAR is currently accessible from a web interface that presents a map overlaid by a circle in motion. Upon finding a given element concealed under the topographical simulation, the system makes a beep sound. By clicking on the discovered element, flagged as a dot marker (a pin) on the map, the readers can watch and listen to a short animation. The animation is created by the ‘Máquina de Ouver [hearing/watching machine]’, a system that translates speech into typographic animation. These speeches are recorded in a database of testimonies from Portuguese poets, writers, musicians and politicians describing the Carnation Revolution (1974) that marks the end of the Portuguese dictatorship period. The circle represents a Sonar, which is activated upon discovering one of the 21 hidden voices declaiming the historic documents. Among the different applications of the Sonar technique to detect and measure objects, from military to scientific and ecological, this work explores the political use, addressing control and censorship. However, instead of using the surveillance technique to spy and silence voices from the resistance, it broadcasts those dissonant voices, identifying and disseminating what was sanctioned and silenced before. The same technique is also used to arrange the order of appearance of the represented testimonies, whose detection is randomized. The work SONAR preserves Portuguese political history and showcases digital technologies as tools for civic mobilization and dissemination of contradicting voices, but also implies that platforms are subject to surveillance and exploitation by antidemocratic forces, namely as enablers for personal data mining.

FIN

#138 怪力亂神New Myth

By John C

EDITORIAL:

New Myth is a combined digital version of two ancient texts of Chinese mythology, 山海經 (ShanHanJing, The Book Of Mountains and Seas) and 博物誌 (BoWuZhi, The Encyclopaedia of Strange Things). These ancient texts are Chinese versions of epics such as The Iliad and The Odyssey, in this case telling the stories of mythical animals and creatures that are often hybrids. The source texts are culturally significant and would be known to intellectual or poetry-loving readers, but are not often taught in schools anymore (except universities) due to their density of language and imagery. The resulting combinatory work New Myth captures some of the fantasy, and is admittedly difficult to read at times--similar to reading Middle English today. “For a long time in China,and I would say even now,” says the author, a university student, “books like those two are described [as] useless, because they write about monsters and non-realistic things, not ‘serious’ theories or ‘useful’ techniques. But in my childhood and even now, they give me a joyful experience.” [Editorial note: this statement is informed by Lai-Tze Fan's review of New Myth. Dr. Fan was an International Consultant to ELC4.]

#141 Sentiment: A Lab Notebook

By Kyle Booten

EDITORIAL:

Using sentiment analysis systems, companies and governments estimate the emotions represented by the words we type on social media platforms and elsewhere. The heart of Booten’s Lab Notebook is a series of poems written in response to the feedback of a machine-learning-powered interface. Using a combination of sentiment analysis and data visualization, this system goads the reader/ writer to perform "emotional oscillation"---to swing wildly from joy to gloom, exaltation to depression. “In the perfect poem,” the Lab Notebook tells us, “emotions flip back and forth,” alternating the emotional current. The Lab Notebook gives one the opportunity to test the emotional amplitude of any written works – poetry; found phrases, nonsense, lyrics to pop songs. As you experiment with Sentiment: a Lab Notebook by submitting text for statistical evaluation, consider testing the “perfect poem” hypothesis by writing (or cutting and pasting) lines that swing between emotional states. Warning: sappy love songs, such as those by the Carpenters, will output a single dot.

#142 improvised is how the voice is used...

By Chris Funkhouser

EDITORIAL:

One of the joys of improvised is how the voice is used . . . is the pauses in Cecil Taylor’s talking as he composes answers to questions about his decades-long career pioneering free jazz. Born in 1929, Taylor (who died in 2018) was known for creating polyrhythms: and that’s exactly what Funkhouser’s ingenious poetry engine has created from an interview he conducted with Taylor in 1994. As the player/auditor simultaneously plays different tracks of Taylor talking, the pauses in Taylor’s speech as he composes an answer are filled, sometimes, by his voice in the concurrently running track. There is no limit to how many tracks the reader/auditor can run simultaneously (up to 52). That level of choice enables productive tension between coherence and sonic density. The engine allows one to create serendipitous discovery. It compresses Taylor’s thinking and allows one to make an entirely new thing. Helpfully tagged by topic, the 52 snippets of varying lengths provide the reader/auditor a basic map of the sonic terrain. For example, a recording of Taylor interviewed at St. Mark’s Church in New York City from 2000 can be layered with one of the recordings from Funkhouser’s interview with him in 1994. As with modernist collage (superimposition), where an ideogram is conceptually stacked and compressed into one new composite, so too these audio collages make a thrilling journey through Taylor’s dazzling career as a mid-to-late twentieth-century, avant-garde Black jazz artist.

#143 A dictionary of the revolution

By Amira Hanafi

EDITORIAL:

Hundreds of people were asked to define the evolving language of the Egyptian revolution that occurred 25 January 2011, the first in a chain of social-media-fueled uprisings that became known as Arab Spring. A dictionary of the revolution is a series of 125 texts woven from the voices of those interviews. The website is beautifully designed, integrating visualization mechanisms that make it easy to access each word by a diagram that shows its relationship to other words. The project documents the rapid amplification of political conversation in the public sphere, in the Habermas’ sense of a society engaged in critical public debate. To engage a large and diverse group of people, author Amira Hanfi created a vocabulary box containing 160 words in colloquial Egyptian that were frequently used between 2011-2013 in public political conversation. In 2014, the artist conducted around 200 conversations with individuals across six Egyptian states: Alexandria, Aswan, Cairo, Mansoura, Sinai and Suez. Choosing cards from the box, people talked about what the words meant to them, who they heard using them, and how their meanings had changed since the uprising. Transcribing these interviews, the artist wove imagined dialogues around each of the words in this populist, crowdsourced "dictionary."

#144 the name is woman

By liliana vasques

EDITORIAL:

The “smiling robot” in Liliana Vasques’s The Name Is Woman challenges our expectation of Instagram poetry as being simple-to-understand. Vasques’s “smiling robot” speaks in opaque aphorisms that make fun of Instagram poetry’s implied ideal lifestyle, such as:

“8:30 buddha awakening/ lift iron/ lift iron/ lift iron/ inner peace. “Lift iron” means a task or chore you need to perform during the day: the “buddha” is ticking off several items on a to-do list then ends the day with “inner peace.” The “smiling robot” is literalized in a self-portrait profile picture, a photograph of wall-mounted sockets for audio equipment. The joke is that, as Scott McCloud noted in his groundbreaking Understanding Comics: The Invisible Art (1994), humans will find reflections of the human face in even the most stripped-down abstraction. So too, Vasques implies, humans will find depth even in Instapoetry that reduces human complexity to quips or slogans. Aesthetically, Vasques plays with glitch, such as blurred-focus videos of previous posts, or chopped, misaligned “robot” self-portraits. The Name Is Woman conjures the “otherness” of Instapoetry pitched at women, a feminist critique of any Instapoem that peddles simplification as empowerment.

FIN

#145 The Deserters

By Laura Okkema

EDITORIAL:

The Deserters is a Twine Game that incorporates many conventional elements of text adventure games into an autobiography. The story is part history, part archaeology, part archival research as the reader/player is tasked with tracking down documents related to the author's family's past. The game is straightforward and uncomplicated; at first glance, this simplicity may make the work feel unsophisticated compared to more experimental interactive works in the four electronic literature Collections. Yet mechanical simplicity is a strength of The Deserters, as it serves rather than distracts from the key purpose of the text: piecing archival documentation together to form a personal and familial history. The text gives one the choice to identify as historian, librarian, or digital humanitarian. The player explores scanned images of historical documents, and reviews translations and explications from the author as lead archivist. In this manner, the reader/player becomes an investigator into history. This is an excellent text to show the adaptability and applicability of interactive media, particularly its ability to bring topics such as history and biography to life. It’s a cross-disciplinary teaching tool, as it intersects history, digital humanities, archiving, German and English language, and biography, as well as employing digital skills, creative writing, and artistic drawings and sketches.

#150 MEMORIAS

By Jessica Arianne Rodríguez Cabrera

MEMORIAS reveals the multiple-threads that make up memory through a reassemblage of text, sounds, and visuals. Playing on the provocative question of how we form our memories, this live installation-as-performative-code poetry uses the browser-based live coding environment Estuary. The result is a blended collaboration of different language-logics to produce compelling audio-visual experiences. Both ephemeral and beautiful, the project explores the complex layers of signification that are constantly shifting in our own experience of time and space.

#167 The Listeners

By John Cayley

EDITORIAL:

What does it mean for our digital "assistants" to listen to us? This unusual project, adopting Alexa/Echo by Amazon, is about control, ownership of network services, and also the future of reading, archives, and literature. The Listeners is a transaction between human speakers and an Amazon Echo. It is also a linguistic performance, installation, and Amazon-distributed third-party app or skill. The Echo embodies a voice-transactive Artificial Intelligence and domestic robot that is named for its wake-word, Alexa. The Listeners is a custom software skill built on top of this infrastructure. This intervention and performance from Cayley and Hatcher asks us to consider all manner of consent: what does it mean for Amazon's AI to "listen" to us, in exchange for the convenience of asking it to play a song or search for a recipe? The naming of the AI as "Alexa" humanizes the robot, making it seem that the AI is a passive, female humanoid servant there to do one's bidding. But it’s also “listening” and directly recording what it hears for its creator, Amazon, building an archive of one’s every fleeting search. Ian Hatcher's vocal performance as the AI is eerie: "We listen for you," it says. "We speak for you.”

#172 Avenue S

By Jody Zellen

EDITORIAL:

The Covid pandemic looms large in this work produced during the height of global lockdowns, when urban streets were eerily silent and empty. Doodles of the empty city and ruminations on the Black Lives Matter protests of summer 2020 resonate here. The cheerful colors are meant to lift spirits even as the work summons spikes in Covid deaths, massive global unemployment, and evacuated public life.
