#173 The Durham Poems

By Benjamin Laird

EDITORIAL:

The Durham Poems is a collection of animated concrete poetry presented in book format concerning William Denton’s childhood and youth (1823-1842) in the County of Durham, UK. It's a lovely contrast to have these slice-of-life poems about a child’s work in the nineteenth century transposed into an animated “book” where the stanzas are not fixed, and the reader can manipulate them to read and dwell. As a child, Denton worked a number of jobs and apprenticeships, first as a courier starting at age eleven and later, at age fourteen, as a machinist in Timothy Hackworth’s workshop. On each reading of this digital chapbook, 15 poems are selected from a list of 23 and each poem is assembled randomly. The reader can drag the poems to alter the way they can be read. The Durham Poems is a thoughtful commentary on how books deliver biography. While biographical poetry is well represented in print, there are few examples in interactive poetry. Reader interactivity and manipulation of the source text troubles the way print lays out in a fixed format the scope of a life; here, in Laird’s work, the contingent qualities of memory and how it (re)assembles what we remember is foregrounded in the randomized structure given to the poems on each read through.

FIN

#176 A Vast and Lonely Desert

By Davis G. See

EDITORIAL:

This walking simulator, made using the free game maker Bitsy, radically expands who gets to make games, and to what use games can be put. While conversation about serious games and Twine games have done a lot to de-center AAA and indie games with high production values as the sine qua non of gaming, A Vast and Lonely Desert takes it further, stripping game making down to mere blocks of color running and triggering conversation; but there’s no threat to “run” from except self-acceptance. Very simple dialog and sonic elements such as the sound of the campfire ironically invoke the lush expansiveness of queer life Walt Whitman glimpses in Brooklyn and Song of Myself. Invoking Whitman, author Davis G. See is freed from making “great” art, but the ironic distance he summons never overwhelms the piece. A Vast and Lonely Desert maps the loneliness of closeted queer life into the metaphor of the desert. Two 8-bit characters find a way to survive, to each other, and something more.

FIN

#178 The Poetry Machine (Ink After Print, Blæk)

By Søren Pold

EDITORIAL:

Casting light on the digitization of literary culture, The Poetry Machine is a participatory, interactive poetry installation. Developed in 2012 as a way for libraries to exhibit electronic literature, the installation consists of three sensor-equipped books through which up to three simultaneous users can compose poems on a screen using hollowed out books with motion detection sensors built inside them. When “seizing” a book, the writer/user is assigned one sentence from this book out of approximately a hundred different sentences. Each sentence exists in three variations, which the writer/user can choose to drag into the writing space. After completion, the user/writer(s) can print their work on small receipts, like a printed receipt for a borrowed library book. Each poem is also stored on a website. The Poetry Machine was designed as a collaborative project between librarians, authors, and researchers. The work focuses on novel forms of collective authorship in embodied, live and fun settings. The installation seeks to make the apparatus of digitization sensible, but it also proposes that digitization does not just make the book disappear into virtual libraries. Rather, it transforms the writing process, how we discover new works to read, and how we connect to other people through a love of books and literature. This work is playable, complex, and iterated over time in ways that reflect the researchers insights about how various groups of people experienced the work. This essential work of elit has been installed in Scandinavian libraries, a rock concert, museums and media art shows. It has been an important discovery tool for many people new to electronic literature.

FIN

#181 partikel (installation)

By jörg piringer

EDITORIAL:

Partikel is a voice-activated installation that generates visual poems from sounds emitted by people visiting the installation. It reflects on the attempts to establish pervasive voice control for devices such as Alexa or Siri, which are marketed as "digital assistants." Unlike these listening systems that benefit corporate profit goals, Partikel doesn't ask participants to subordinate one's own speech to utilitarian computer systems or the tech industry’s economic structures. Partikel expands the sound and language possibilities of the voice by exploring, as so much of Piringer’s work has, connections between sound and visual representation of words. Visitors control the visual and acoustic events through their voices, and the artwork reacts dynamically: sound influences the image, and the image reciprocally influences the sound. The output to kinetic typography builds upon Piringer's extensive catalog of such works, of which the early mobile apps abcdefghijk . . . and konsonant, (circa 2010) are just two examples.

FIN

#182 All the Delicate Duplicates

By Mez Breeze

EDITORIAL:

All the Delicate Duplicates is a short narrative game that toys with the concept of time, offering the reader/player an opportunity to interact with objects left behind by the two main characters, and piece together the conditions of their lives. John, a computer engineer, inherits a collection of arcane objects from his aunt. Over time, the engineer and his daughter begin to realize that the objects have unusual physical properties. The more they are exposed to these objects, the more the characters’ realities and memories appear to change. All the Delicate Duplicates repurposes familiar first-person shooter game mechanics in this psychologically complex and evocative walking simulator. Using a mouse/keyboard and/or gamepad, players/readers can explore objects, diaries, journals, newspaper cuttings, mobile phones, laptops and other items left in this surreal setting that changes in relationship to how the player interacts with it.

FIN

#185 The Fetch

By Jerome Fletcher

EDITORIAL:

Live performance of The Fetch at the 2013 Electronic Literature Organization conference in Paris demonstrated the thrill of live reading that triggered a hunt for “found objects” on the web. The Fetch, a Gaelic word for a wraith or doppelganger, projected digital texts that are read by one performer while the second performer searches the net for texts which use the same combination of four word groups in the projected text. In this sense, The Fetch is a formula anyone can replicate for making a lived experience of the heterogeneity of the web, stitched together through hyperlinks, tags and hashtags. While others have memorably documented such heterogeneity (one thinks of Cayley and Howe’s How It Is In Common Tongues, 2012), The Fetch “haunts” the original texts pulled from websites where the same sequence of words appear--but often in a completely different setting. Conceptual writing that interrogates the web as our digital commons of palimpsestic traces. The Fetch can be played, but some of the links are broken--link rot on the web as a decaying house.

FIN

#186 The Wonders of Lost Trajectories

By Jason Nelson

EDITORIAL:

How to tell the story of a place? How to make a state’s archives lively and interactive? Jason Nelson was the digital-poet-in-residence of Queensland, the large state in the northeastern corner of the continent; the Great Barrier Reef is just offshore. The Wonders of Lost Trajectories delves into how we discern what’s worth remembering, how lived experience of a place evolves over time—and how to make archives relevant and experiential for those who inhabit the space today. Nelson created poetry, fiction, and interactive texts inspired by or directly informed from materials in the state archives. Each of the seven works was specifically designed for the building in which they were exhibited to visitors. These works revivified now-decommissioned library archival equipment such as a card catalogue cabinet, microfilm readers, and long, wooden work tables. Nelson transformed these objects into vehicles for digital fiction and poetry. It’s a brilliant example of location-specific (“locative”) eliterature, where the work invites people to experience their surroundings through interactive, literary experience.

FIN

#187 Liza Gennart

By Zuzana Husárová

EDITORIAL:

Liza Gennart is an artificial intelligence that writes emotive poetry. Trained on contemporary Slovak poetry and on a vast corpora of Slovak sources from the web, Liza Gennart’s book Výsledky vzniku (“Outcomes of Origin”) writes poems about humanity, maternity, nature and technology. The name “Liza Gennart” was made by combining the initials of the humans who wrote the AI (Zuzana Husárová and Ľubomír Panák) and a concatenation of the phrase “generative art.” In one of the poems, titled "I’m Not a Robot," Liza Gennart reflects on “her” own ontological status. Publication of the book Výsledky vzniku followed the typical production cycle of a high-profile printed poetry collection, including marketing via author interviews, public readings, and radio broadcasts that showcased the emotive quality of the poems and emphasized that "Liza Gennart" is the AI "daughter" of the authors, who also have two human daughters. Enthusiastic reception in Slovakia centered on the book's unusual human/AI mode of production and poetics, and resulted in the human authors becoming laureates of the Slovak National Poetry Prize Zlatá Vlna for this collection Výsledky vzniku. Since the limited edition printed book sold all copies and is no longer available for purchase, the authors offer a PDF of the poetry volume to readers of ELC4.

FIN

#190 Give Me a Reason

By Terhi Marttila

EDITORIAL:

This piece was developed together with a community of volunteers who work with refugees near Munich, Germany in 2015-2016. Give Me a Reason is multilingual, using Google Translate to make the testimonies available in dozens of languages. What motivates people to welcome immigrants and work to help settle them? The author and her collaborator organized dialogues with the German volunteers (of several ages, genders and nationalities) where they reflected on their experiences. Each participant contributed 8 reasons for seeking contact with and helping the refugees. These reasons were spliced into groups of verbs, objects and subjects. The "Give Me a Reason" button randomly selects snippets to create infinite new reasons for helping refugees. This piece was born during a year when Germany was in the process of absorbing about one million refugees largely from the Middle East. Besides serving as an insight into the psyche and demographics of the Germans who sought contact with the newcomers, this work is a never-ending supply of reasons why people volunteer to help when strangers arrive seeking support and refuge. As with the Taroko Gorge collection in Electronic Literature Collection Volume 3, the hit-and-miss quality of this generator’s output is part of what makes this piece interactively literary. Parsing the recombinant reasons, the reader’s mind fills in the gaps to make sense of an overwhelming amount of information.

FIN

#192 hearing litoral voices / bearing literal traces : Subliteral Narratives

By John Cayley and Joanna Howard

EDITORIAL:

Subliteral Narratives is “slow” electronic literature. It’s a work you can put on and let run in the background, checking it whenever the mood strikes you. The “subliteral” refers to tiny changes in a word’s meaning when, in certain fonts, differences of less-than-a-letter distinguish certain pairs of English words. Think about the tiny empty space at the bottom of the letter “h” that is fully rounded in the letter “b,” for example. The work’s profundity emanates from the large shifts in semantic meaning that these tiny font differences conjure. Add to that the palimpsestic writing and erasure of this piece’s encoded short narrative passages that work in semantic tension with each vignette’s fixed, situational frameworks such as "ARS POETICA: on the origins of collaboration, on material difference, on the giving up of one novel for another” and "On awaiting the trial of a poor girl having murdered a pastor with a fire iron, Portsmouth, 1818." The many material layers of this work, from the typographic, to the intricate code, to its elegant monochromatic aesthetic reward careful attention.

FIN

#195 Exploration of Anonymous History

By David Clark

EDITORIAL:

Marshall McLuhan, Canadian engineer and media visionary, imagined how media interact with the human sensorium. In doing so, he unleashed our imagination of how humans write, read and listen through techne. David Clark’s Exploration of Anonymous History makes ample reference to the themes McLuhan was in the process of developing in an innovative interdisciplinary journal Explorations, published in Toronto (1953-1959). Using a vocabulary of interactive comic books to create dynamic collages and a non-linear experience of the text, Clark makes McLuhan’s still-resonant ideas spring to life through interaction with selected themes such as “metaphor,” “mechanization,” “simultaneous” and “obsolete.” Fans of Clark’s iconic 88 Constellations for Wittgenstein (2008) will recognize in Exploration of Anonymous History the collage aesthetic, cinematic cuts and multilayered soundscape, this time bent toward the purpose of providing interactive experience of McLuhan’s boldly exploratory work in the 1950s, before his books during the 1960s spawned media studies. Taking inspiration from a companion program of scholarly research about the Explorations journal by fellow Canadians Janine Marchessault and Michael Darroch, Clark’s artistic exploration of the archival and database-centered experiences of the mid-twentieth century techne in the age of the internet demonstrates how scholarly research can discover new dimensions of meaning by offering also interactive experiences populated by 3D graphics, snippets of films, and audio interpretations of the text.

FIN

#197 Uncertainty Index

By Sarah Ciston

EDITORIAL:

Uncertainty Index is a data-driven poetic investigation and interactive poem that discloses to the reader how data surveillance is quietly shaping both our social structures and our private lives. Toggling between the quantified self and the ruminative self via a combination of code and lyric language, readers scroll through a journal-like stream of bodily metadata and poetic fragments. The complexity of the work lies in the critical insight it yields when exposing potential bias and ideological leanings that are baked into algorithmic engines and data tracking processes, insight disclosed in the work of data feminists like Safiya Umojai Noble, and the team of Catherine D’Ignazio and Lauren Klein. Despite the democratizing promise of digital technologies, identity markers are reinforced and even extracted as capital through (in)voluntary participation in algorithmic systems. Uncertainty Index is a canny feminist intervention at the nexus of data surveillance, body image, and oversharing on social media. This piece makes us consider how digital affordances make an understanding of “self” either more or less accessible, as the technological intimacies of our tracked selves continue to be harvested in web 2 “social” interfaces.

FIN

#200 Tiny Protests / Protestitas

By Leonardo Flores

EDITORIAL:

Tiny Protests / Protestitas is a suite of generative bots that reflect the challenging times we find ourselves in. It consists of five iterations of activist expression. @TinyProtests is a Twitter bot that generates U.S. themed marches and protests. @Protestitas is a fork from the original @TinyProtests that generates Puerto Rican themed protests. Tiny Protests / Protestitas is also a minimalist piece published in Taper #2 that brings the first two bots together into a single, endless march. Also included is the ultra-minimalist version made for NaNoGenMo (National Novel Generation Month). This iteration of the work generates a 1,334 page march, calling for Trump's impeachment. Finally, the most recent manifestation is @CyberProtests, which offers emoji representations of online protest in response to the COVID-19 quarantine and lockdown orders. Perhaps more political than literary, this is a “living project” which deploys algorithmic protest to comment on contemporary political turmoil. Participatory in both sentiment and design, Tiny Protests / Protestitas has expanded to new contexts, finding a wider critical audience for this form of elit expression.

FIN

#202 .break .dance

By Marisa Parham

EDITORIAL:

.break .dance is an experimental digital project, described in part as a pocket, a place, a position, and a place for experimentation in form and content. The work is also posited as “a thing behind a thing, the thing you hold on to, just in case”. An elusive and exciting piece that defies categorization despite its roots in the broader field of the digital humanities, it is a “tiny universe of intellectual possibility,” Parham notes. Beyoncé’s visual album Lemonade serves as a keystone text to ground musings about time, code, and internet experience. Situated at the intersection of cultural analytics and hemispheric American slavery, break .dance includes discussions of Flying Lotus’ “Never Catch Me (ft. Kendrick Lamar)”, Toni Morrison's portrayal of Baby Suggs in Beloved, “Formation” by Beyoncé, and Becky (Cane) by Jean Toomer. It includes images, animations and fragments of videos as it captures displacement and loss as well as resilience and the recodification of time and space. A slow reading project, break .dance uses a fading/disappearing technique to meditate on the legacy of slavery.

FIN

#204 A Slow Year

By Ian Bogost

EDITORIAL:

“Game poems aspire toward a kind of videogame version of Imagism,” notes author-programmer Bogost, “if we expand ‘image’ to include a logic or behavior as its subject.” Invoking the high modernism of Ezra Pound, Bogost juxtaposes the interactive dynamism of videogames to the deliberate stillness of A Slow Year, a collection of four games representing the weather of autumn, winter, spring and summer. If Imagism packed meaning into a condensed images using the technique of superposition, then the procedural rhetoric of these “slow” Atari games asks the one to sit with stillness and contemplation at the very console that brought frenetic, joystick-intensive gameplay from the arcade into the home. A Slow Year is beautiful, its minimalist evocations of being in outside in nature exactly the opposite of the 1980s gamer’s physical situation in a room with all attention focused on a screen. As poems, the vignettes of A Slow Year inspire rumination about how humans have always interacted with imaginative work.

FIN

#208 Hana Feels

By Gavin Inglis

EDITORIAL:

Hana Feels is a role-playing work of hypertext digital fiction that places the reader/player in four roles related to Hana, who is experiencing a mental crisis. The narrative progresses through conversations with Hana as different characters attempt to guide her through a rough patch. More didactic than literary, Hana Feels is a great example of elit with an applied purpose: to provide young adults a robust, interactive setting to take the measure of a crisis and model problem solving. The story has three endings, showing that what people say to Hana makes a difference in her state of mind and influences her behavior.

FIN

#217 Thoughts and Prayers: The Game

By Mike Lacher, Chris Baker, and Brian Moore.

EDITORIAL:

This 30-second game occasions a literary experience through the frustration it generates. Using real-life hashtags gathering Tweets commemorating the victims of mass shootings in the United States, this point-and-click game gives the player the option to “think” or “pray” in reaction to yet another mass murder hashtag. Speedthroughs will only get you faster to the “Ban Assault Weapon Sales” button, which triggers scathing reminders of how beholden elected officials are to the National Rifle Association’s campaign donations. Aesthetically reminiscent of Cory Arcangel’s Super Mario Clouds (2002), Thoughts and Prayers uses that aesthetic to mock the political gridlock that prevents any kind of meaningful solution to the epidemic of gun violence. Old-school arcade sounds and visuals remind us of how long we’ve lived with mass murders as if they were an inevitable part of daily life, rather than a choice.

FIN

#218 "Why are the Digital Humanities So Straight?"

By Edmond Y. Chang

EDITORIAL:

Why are the Digital Humanities So Straight? is an academic essay-as-parser game, setting the reader on a course to unlock secrets about Alan Turing, Ada Lovelace and Purna Jackson, a fictional character from Techland's 2001 Dead Island games. As a mash-up of fiction/non-fiction that explores the “technonormativity of code”, this work offers a special blend of scholarly critical analysis by playing a text-based game in BASIC.

FIN

#219 Aleph Null 3.0

By Jim Andrews

EDITORIAL:

Aleph Null 3.0 is an online, interactive, generative art engine and tool for creating images and animations that have a distinct “look”. An online graphic synthesizer, it samples and mashes up graphics and uses those visual samples as “paint” to create real-time animations that synthesize images. Using Aleph Null 3.0 is part exploration, part adventure. It is also serious remix fun. As interactive net art, it invites us all to play with the visual detritus of the internet, and serves as a participatory artistic medium that can spark the imagination. As creator Jim Andrews states in his “minifesto” for the work, “The Internet will be exciting only so long as it remains inspiring to artists—as an artistic medium. If that light goes out, the forces of dullness will have secured the entire thing as a department store, surveillance device and peep show.”

FIN

#221 progress in work

By Bruno Ministro

EDITORIAL:

Progress in work is a provocative piece which denounces, in a creative and blunt manner, the poor work conditions suffered by people employed by the Amazon Mechanical Turk projects. Such projects crowdsource the labor marketplace by outsourcing microtasks to a distributed/temporary workforce. The piece uses random text and image combinations generated by MTurk workers (related to Amazon Mechanical Turk projects). Each user that took part in this “virtually distributed workforce” (to quote Amazon) was paid USD $ 0.05 per task, known as HITs (Human Intelligence Tasks). The piece inherently refers to the conditions of underemployment and exploitation that go hand in hand with digital capitalism. Addressing timely concerns regarding the revolution of "work" in the age of computer automation and data politics, the ideogrammatic approach here creates unexpected exchanges between text and image, and yields a profound sense of defamiliarization that is a hallmark of the globalization of labor. The source texts being used, in multiple languages and pertinent to the topics under scrutiny, establish a reflexive dialogue with the pictures/photographs of workers and their work environments, allowing a reflexive reading/seeing activity.

FIN

#223 Radical of the Vertical Hand 忄

By Daniel Howe

EDITORIAL:

Radical of the Vertical Heart 忄 is the latest work in the generative and conceptual literature series that the author calls “Atomic Language Machines”. This reading machine searches the Chinese lexicon by repeatedly making minimal changes (stroke-by-stroke) to the sub-character components of characters, in order to arrive at a new word. When the machine lands on sensitive words, such as those disallowed by China's Great Firewall, a break occurs. The work is a powerful reminder of the diverse ways in which machine reading parses combinatorial meaning in text/language. Radical of the Vertical Heart忄 has appeared alongside "Automatype" in an installation context. The simultaneous exploration/interaction with English machines is an important comparative approach: words mutate via the smallest number of possible mutations, by means of "deletion, addition, or substitution". Analogously, the Chinese machines assess the proximity of characters and words by analyzing "strokes, radicals, and semantic/phonemic sub-components". Side by side, they expose the particularity in different linguistic structures along with the machine’s capacity to pattern these distinctions, exposing very different meaning-making processes derived from sinographic versus alphabetic traditions. With this work, there is an implicit critique of algorithmic and machine reading of both the logogram and the alphabet. What do these reading machines search for, and what does it mean that they seem never to be satisfied?

FIN

#225 Textos Guerreros / Words of Guerrero

By Pablo Somonte Ruano

EDITORIAL:

Words of Guerrero is a linguistic experiment and a provocation, privileging a local lexicon and a familiar discursive understanding over the ideological overreach of governmental structures of control. Based on how linguistic structure, content, and grammar relate in public spaces, the piece employs a propaganda slogan of the Mexican government, and programs it anew in order to allow readers to recombine words and photographs. The experiment replaces instructions for the general Mexican public with the local lexicon of Guerrero, rejecting the government’s heavy hand. Words of Guerrero foregrounds the recent push of gentrification in many downtown neighborhoods in Mexico and around the world, and highlights the visualization of subtle (and not so subtle) ways of resistance. The photos (painted signs, advertisements, warnings, graffiti) are the basis for a textual remix, using a cut-up technique. The resulting political and cultural context of such détournement is a clever overturn due to the combinatorial blend of language and visual artifacts.

FIN

#226 Byderhand-Pioneer Project

By Franci Greyling

EDITORIAL:

Byderhand-Pioneer Project is an engaging multidisciplinary project that uses locative literature to create a poetic installation at a school for the visually impaired in Worcester in the Western Cape of South Africa. In a multisensory garden on the school grounds, one can access “The Garden Verses” - a poetry collection of multimodal verse linked by an auditory offering. A user-centered and co-design approach was applied to design the multimodal and multilevel interface, and the collection includes ten poems that are experienced in multiple languages and media. The design also includes the combination of braille, QR codes and an accessible user interface that makes provision for sighted, visually impaired and blind users. This special installation can indeed be understood as “applied electronic literature studies”. It is distinct because the multimodal literary installations are accessible to persons with visual impairment, but also because persons with visual impairment played an integral role in the design and co-creation of the project.

#227 (DES)CONEXÃO

By wr3ad1ng d1g1t5

EDITORIAL:

(DES)CONEXÃO [Dis-connection] is a collaborative artistic project that blends physical and virtual interactions, analog and digital media, mythical and scientific principles. Initially developed as an installation, the current iterations are documented on the web, providing background context that allows readers to approach the artwork in its full heterogeneity. The project adopts an alchemical allegory, compelling us to think about time at a moment when instant access and immediate gratification are the rule. Digital media support modification and multiplication, indulging in all forms of metamorphosis, deformation, and even alchemy. In this case, discovery and revelation imply a cumulative (algorithmic) and procedural (interactive) attitude from the initiate, called upon to take part in the gradual decoding of the artifact. Proposing an approximation between the alchemical method and forms of digital interaction may seem a strange endeavor, but after following the four alchemical steps in the project, the readers will be able to answer for themselves: 1) #DECOMPOSITION is the installation of the work in a public space: fully interactive, promoting attachment and collaborative co-production of meaning; 2) #MODIFICATION presents and dissects the work at an academic conference, without displaying the digital component itself, aimed at what lies “behind the surface of the artifact;” 3) #SEPARATION concerns the pedagogical outreach, exhibiting and circulating the work in schools; 4) #UNION is the final contact with the artifact itself, a circular interactive digital interface that links to 32 different media works, where readers can bring what they have discovered in the previous steps, finding it had been within themselves all along.

FIN

#229 Robbo. Solucja / Robbo. Walkthrough

By Piotr Marecki

EDITORIAL:

Robbo. Solucja / Robbo. Walkthrough documents an important phenomenon for a generation of Polish programmers who came of age hacking the Atari system. A work made in 2017, Robbo Walkthrough is a hybrid piece: a text generator made within the Atari system that was then outputted to a printed game walkthrough which included tips on how to beat the popular game Robbo. All of the elements of this work–text, music, code, composition, and graphics–were created by Atari enthusiasts on original machines. Piotr Marecki calls this endeavor “zombie” computing: reviving a “dead” technology incompatible with today’s gaming systems but still capable of supporting creative programming. Zombie computing on “dead” media shows that the perpetual drive for new technology is a choice, not a necessity. Robbo Walkthrough is a deliberately nonsensical rendition of a walkthrough, though it does supply actual clues for how to beat the Robbo game. An in-joke for those who remember Robbo, which teenage Polish hackers programmed on tiny bits of unused space on Atari game cassettes, Robbo Walkthrough is, for everyone else, a retro glimpse into how digital culture was made during Poland’s communist era, when access to personal computers was extremely scarce.

FIN

#230 Dial

By Lai-Tze Fan

EDITORIAL:

Dial incorporates the environment and stylings of what has become, for some of us, our dominant form of communication: digital dialogue. Created in the context of 2020’s global pandemic resulting in physical and social isolation, it expresses the tenuous lifeline offered through texting and IMing. The dialogue is generative, varying through emojis and brief phrases conveying weather, seasons, and the passage of time, the two voices coalesce into something of a monologue. Clicking the clocks on the bottom of the work adjust the time in the piece, but this effect is fleeting and, at times, confusing—a deeper reflection on the malleable time experienced during lockdowns, when minutes can feel like days, and months pass with no discernable memory to separate them. The work is a remarkable generative recreation of a rather global experience.

FIN

#231 The Infinite Catalog of Crushed Dreams

By Mark Sample

EDITORIAL:

The Infinite Catalog of Crushed Dreams is an endless stream of procedurally generated sadness, frustration, and grief. It captures the collective weight of so many disappointments when all is called off and the unfathomable is actually unfolding, highlighting both the local impasses as well as the global scale of the coronavirus pandemic. This randomly generated list goes on forever, using an infinite scrolling feature. Paradoxically, it is very sad and very funny at the same time, which results in a reading experience of estrangement. An apt snapshot of elit pandemic fiction.

FIN

#232 TheWorldIsNotDoneYet

By Annie Grosshans

EDITORIAL:

The World in Not Done Yet is a poignant cross-perspective memoir and narrative, a tapestry of familial and community storytelling that pays tribute to print literacies while remediating them in the digital context. It is an intimate portrait of the way we inherit both memory and connection, and it presses us to think about the ways in which we learn to share meaning. The World is Not Done Yet also considers the conventions we have learned to live by - the framing and colonizing narratives that have kept certain knowledge unsaid - and it yields to make way for new modes and new voices. In short, the work composes a revised inheritance. Multi voices weave in and out like the downstream of utterances that flow from a certain origin. This expressive and innovative piece embraces multimodality and crosses the boundaries of fiction, poem, memoir, art, history, and criticism. It posits the idea of new literacies while establishing a new kind of literary experience as fluid, spherical connectivity.

FIN

#233 Please Answer Carefully

By litrouke

EDITORIAL:

Please Answer Carefully is a Twine game that seems like a generalized web survey but later reveals itself as a psychological horror game. It is a playful experience that lures the respondent into certain familiar expectations while deceptively changing the terms of the engagement. This short yet clever little game takes the premise of the web survey and brings into surprisingly meaningful territory. A great example of how the hypertext interface can use familiar mediated conventions to create new forms of storytelling.

FIN

#237 A Modern Ghost

By Artemio Morales

EDITORIAL:

A Modern Ghost is an example of a digital short story as app, using text-image dialogue while remediating graphic novels and illustrated books. Created for iOS and Android, it employs artwork with a clean, black and white contrast aesthetic while exploring the use of a 3D canvas to create a distinct sense of place. Vertical and horizontal controls offer the reader the ability to explore via Scott McCloud’s concept of the “infinite scroll”. As a work aiming at a commercial market, this is the kind of piece that may hold potential to draw new readers into the world of electronic literature.

FIN

#240 Powieki (Eyelids)

By Zenon Fajfer

EDITORIAL:

The intricate, multi-leveled, acrostic structure of Powieki is an expanded and complicated version of "the emanational poem," an innovative poetic form created by Fajfer. The poem is traversed through a "slow reading" hypertextual experience. Powieki constitutes an almost optimal hypertext, using temporal links and conditional links to creatively exploit the hypertextual rhetoric in its patterns and motifs. Powieki is a crucial example of Polish electronic poetry. Mariusz Pisarski, a literary critic of Polish eliterature, wrote in his review of the work that it is “an oasis of zen in the world of hysterical discourses, offering us a verbal therapy on the liberatic couch.” "Liberature" is a concept of haptic, playable printed or handmade books articulated by Fajfer in a 1999 manifesto of the same name. This manifesto launched a movement in Poland that has now stretched internationally and combined with other forms of print-based “physical” literature, in the phrase of publishing scholar Simon Rowberry. "Liberatic" analysis of elit and playable books flourishes in Poland and beyond, thanks to the formal inventions, library curation, and cultural stewardship of Fajfer and literary critic Katarzyna Bazarnik. [Editorial note: this statement is informed by Dr. Monika Górska-Olesińska’s review of Powieki. Dr. Górska-Olesińska was an International Consultant to ELC4.]

#242 We Descend, Volume II

By Bill Bly

EDITORIAL:

We Descend Volume II is an ongoing literary hypertext whose first volume was developed in 1997 using Eastgate Systems’ proprietary software Storyspace, and whose second volume was published on the open web in 2017. This haptic experience in ELC4 is media archeology. Originally published on floppy disk and marketed to readers of “serious” literature in a rectangular cardboard box that suggested a book, We Descend: Archives Pertaining to Egderus Scriptor is acknowledged to be a classic early hypertext. We Descend is a historical fiction told through an archive of diaries, letters, and confessions discovered by the protagonist, Egderus, a young boy isolated at a mountain house containing these artifacts, some of which are hundreds of years old. Author Bill Bly, like many early hypertext writers, used the story concept of the personal, generational archive to distinguish hypertext’s functional difference from printed books. Instead of following a sequence of chapters laid out in a printed book, readers of early hypertext could sample and traverse the archive of artifacts, piecing together stories, fragments and mysteries as they develop across generations. In 2017, We Descend Volume II appeared on the web in longtime elit journal The New River. Volume Two continues the exploration of writing artifacts linked through hypertext, a browsable (fictional) archive that discloses mysterious interconnections the farther one “descends” into the archive.

#243 Remixing Shakespeare: A Netprov in Three Acts

By Joellyn Rock

EDITORIAL:

Multimodal and a mix of staged video and textual improvisation, this netprov (“networked, improvised literature”) repurposes experimental videos originally created for Remixing Shakespeare, a collaborative live performance staged at Karpeles Manuscript Museum in honor of the national tour of Shakespeare's First Folio. The video project was a partnership with The Folger Shakespeare Library, University of Minnesota Duluth, and KUMD radio. Remixing Shakespeare is an ongoing project, where site visitors can add to the work using either a Google Form built into the author’s website or specific Twitter hashtags focusing on character contests from Shakespeare as they mix up with the power-plays of our own cultural moment. This exercise is highly adaptable. It could even be run in a classroom with students typing into a simple Google doc as they engage in repartee prompted by the video. Players are encouraged to borrow liberally from Shakespeare and from social media, remixing characters and scenarios that may illuminate or throw shade on current events--without naming real names, only literary ones.

#249 The Warp and Weft of Memory

By Renée Turner

EDITORIAL:

This well-written and nicely designed piece invites its readers to explore the life of Dutch artist Gisèle d’Ailly van Waterschoot van der Gracht through the artifacts she left behind. Multiple media—photos, videos, drawings—and the epistolary exchanges of the work’s creators about her life, converge to form biographical documentation of the woman artist. In doing so, the work leads us through “the intimacies of her closet”, while exposing broader pictures of her environment, her society, and her nation during periods of peace and war. #251 V[R]ignettes: A Microstory Series

By Mez Breeze

EDITORIAL:

V[R]ignettes is a VR anthology in the genre of high fantasy. Readers/players can use the touchpad to zoom into the 3D model, spinning, rotating or otherwise shifting it to gain perspective on the fantastical creatures. Breeze tags snippets of story to different parts of the 3D model. There are also arrow keys that jump to each tagged snippet if the reader wishes a guided form of exploration. The reading experience is to toggle between examining the volumetric dimensions of the modeled creature or phenomenon, then reading Breeze’s signature enigmatic prose written in an English-based language she invented in the 1990s called mezangelle. V[R]ignettes is a microstory universe where each individual vignette explores the literary connection between kinetic actions/mechanics and textual evocations. At once exploratory and forensic–readers of Breeze’s large body of literary works will be rewarded by diving into and pursuing continuitites among the works she’s made over 30 years–V[R]ignettes boldly limns what’s possible in the “extended reality” [XR] of 3D literary environments.

#252 my Dear coUntess

By Danny Snelson

EDITORIAL:

This hypervideo work from 2007 is dadaist elit - a word-by-word rainbow recomposition of Alfred Jarry's famous letter to Lord Kelvin in Exploits and Opinions of Dr. Faustroll, Pataphysician. Every word is color-coded and leads to a source text accompanied by different prerecorded video fragments. #255 Kjell Theory

By Judd Morrissey

EDITORIAL:

Kjell Theøry is a work of augmented reality [AR] elit and theatrical performance installed in many different locations: theaters, public plazas, and city landmarks in Bergen, Norway. The AR technology works by pinning story elements to geo-spatial tags that pop up AR animations, triggered by a participant’s eye motions or other interaction. Using hyperlinked tattoos inked on performers’ bodies, AR animations are layered onto the highly choreographed performers, who are both physically performing for the audience and projected onto a screen (such as a large screen behind the players, or an app on a smart device). Kjell Theøry explores resonances between Alan Turing’s queerness and the Greek myth of Tiresias, Apollo’s blind prophet who was both man and woman. Turing’s travels to Norway took place after estrogen treatments imposed on him as punishment for crimes of homosexual “indecency” in the UK caused gynecomastia, the growth of male breasts. Kjell Theøry explores the role of location during this last phase of Turing’s life. The production history of Kjell Theøry illustrates the precariousness of authoring in new, transient technical systems. Kjell Theøry was made with Layar, an app that suddenly folded and became instantly obsolete. As is the case with Caitlin Fisher’s 200 Castles (also documented in this ELC4 Collection), early AR elit is not replicable but is nevertheless a critical turning point in the field that merits documentation and study.

#257 Quauhnáhuac

By Leonardo Aranda Brito, et al.

EDITORIAL:

Quahnáhuac is a multimedia work blending photo montage, sound, and a circular navigation system that remediates Malcolm Lowry’s modernist classic Under the Volcano in a Spanish translation, Bajo el volcán. Quahnáhuac uses the language of Lowry’s text to speak back against the colonization of Mexico. Lowry’s original text depicts the point-of-view of an alcoholic British consul living in the small town of Quahnáhuac, the Indigenous name for what is now known as Cuernavaca. Readers can inhabit a casino, theater, two palaces, garden, plaza, and a gully in photos that look antique but also mention present day class struggles. The photo collage anchoring the Casino lexia, for example, includes protest signs that say “Fuera Costco del casino” (“Costco, get out of the casino”). A cartography of place and time, the navigation of Quahnáhuac is a “wheel of fortune,” putting readers in the position of the alcoholic consul’s delirium. Readers are embedded in real settings to tell the story of the same city from colonial plans that reveal urban transformations of Indigenous land.

#260 Golden Days, Silver Nights

By Brian Greenspan

EDITORIAL:

Golden Days, Silver Nights is a locative work of augmented reality made non-locative and web-accessible for pandemic-enabled visitation. Its locative version employs AR and projected cinema reels portraying its historical political events, prompted by hotspots on Carleton University in Ottawa, Canada. The narrative, as the artist statement notes, is set in the 1896 American election between William Jennings Bryan and William McKinley, and is extremely well-researched and presented in multiple media. The “remote” or web version places the player on an interactive map of the university campus; positioning the arrow avatar over a shaded or tinted section (functioning as the locative hotspots) triggers photos, audio, and video conveying the events of the time, including the darker undercurrents of racism and imperialist attitudes. This work is an excellent example of how mobile apps and AR are being used for history, heritage, and tourism around the world, exciting users and porting them back in time and place.

#267 200 Castles

By Caitlin Fisher

EDITORIAL:

Augmented Reality eliterature uses the camera on a smartphone or tablet to detect “tagged” objects that trigger animations overlaid atop the object. The result is a “magical” sensation that ordinary objects can behave in extraordinary ways, such as in 200 Castles when a printed book about the history of a castle seems to contain animations and audio that tell memorable tales about the inhabitants of the castle across time. Episodic and non-linear, 200 Castles marks the beginning moments of AR elit (see also, in this collection, Judd Morrissey’s Kjell Theøry), before AR became a mainstream technology used in museum exhibits and advertising. The interaction between a material object and the “magic looking glass” of the smartphone or tablet animations and sounds isn’t possible to replicate in this collection. Nevertheless, such work is important to field development as Fisher and other artists pushed the technology to unlock stories of human memory and desire. The author notes: “Contemporary sex scenes, mannered tales of hoarding, war stories and poetry blend to present a larger story of a physical space filled with stories over time.”

#268 Latino-American literary mirror: and experiment with Machine Learning

By Mario Guzman

EDITORIAL:

Latino-American Literary Mirror: an Experiment with Machine Learning is conceptual writing overlaid with a soundtrack that includes slow percussion and ambient street sounds, such as an ambulance. As the reader attempts to find patterns in the flickering cells zoomed out to make a pixelated picture at macroscopic scale, those flashing tiny boxes are created by machines trained in literary texts based on neural networks. It is an experiment in “endless writing” and reading, where sampling the visual output triggers associations in the reader’s mind rather than defining an explicit reading experience. An exercise in mediation, reading, and knowledge production in networked computational environments, Latino-American Literary Mirror invites the reader to search for traces of the human and the cultural in this machinic landscape. Using a generative language model trained on 19th-century travel literature, the work is a meeting of faces and images of migratory movements. Travel as a metaphor for the human reach for novel experiences and new-to-them cultures is matched in this work that mashes up the migratory, the machinic, and the human desire to find connection with that which is initially strange.

#270 Yardley, PA 1997

By Todd Anderson

EDITORIAL:

Invoking an ethereal midsummer’s night dream, Yardley, PA 1997 is an interactive poem that beckons the reader with fireflies in an evening sky and an ambient soundscape that chimes and pulses. Each line of this mash-up poem is bound to a keystroke with an accompanying sound clip. The reader soon discovers that while playing with their keyboard, they can arrange the poem’s stanzas to produce a layered lexia-screenscape along with a compelling sound symphony. This piece can be played individually, or showcased in public. The work must be especially appealing in an installation or as live performance, as the composition lends itself to interactive public reading.

#272 Coal Code

By Kenneth Sherwood

EDITORIAL:

A poetics of place, Coal Code is self-reflexive (an “auto-documentary”) that uses layers of spoken word testimonies to emplace the reader in a timeline that’s both historical and contemporary where coal is mined in western Pennsylvania. Through retro user keyboard controls (Random, Sequential, Duet, Gaps), the reader can navigate the listening environment and be provoked to think about the specific history of the land where one currently lives. This was the case for author Kenneth Sherwood, who mined his local history to discover stories of coal that involve “lads 4-10 years old” and encompass the sweep of the Industrial Revolution, right up to present-day when coal “powers the digital machines with which I make my art.” Original and found texts are live remixed by the reader/listener. Mouse clicks trigger audio and tiles of antique, regional postcards that make a grid of windows into a local past that still manifests in our computational present.

#273 Bastardo

By David Núñez

EDITORIAL:

Bastardo is combinatorial digital fiction and a dynamic hyperliterature “system” that mixes diverse sets of lexia to create a multitude of different stories. The narrative cohesion of so many story fragments (10x149 different texts) hinges on short prose pieces as “blocks” governed by specific narrative rules. The fragmented nodes are like pieces of a story-plot puzzle, bound by preconstructed coherence determined not by the algorithm, but by human author. Nonetheless, the code scrambles and reconstructs narrative order in iterations anew resulting in different approaches and resolutions, delivering each reader a unique book by using digital combinatorial processes. This transformation of the fixed relation to plot forces us to apprehend the compelling tension between the generativity of the machine alongside the hermeneutic insight of a human reader.

#274 Voz Pública

By Dora Ytzell Bartilotti Bigurra

EDITORIAL:

Voz Pública or “Public Voice” is a dynamic participatory art piece that addresses historical discrimination and seeks to make visible the problem of gender violence in the urban context of Latin America. It is made up of three interconnected elements: An online platform for gathering and visualizing anonymous contributions from women and non-binary people that were victims of violence; electronic textile that is displayed in public space; and a series of urban laboratories called “La Rebelión Textil” which are meant as spaces for reflection hosting maker workshops and activist meetings. The online participation and visualization platform invites people to share (textually and anonymously) their personal stories. These narratives in turn become the creative foundation for the electronic textiles produced with an embedded computing system and stitched together with conducive thread securing voice synthesizers in micro-speakers. The electronic textiles are also a visual reference to the Latin American textile tradition. Electronic textiles are made into garments and in turn “activated” in protest. They are worn to public spaces such as parks, squares, streets and public transport, amplifying voices and making visible personal testimonials, while situating the narrator-activists as collective representatives for the victims of violence. A powerful and provocative blend of corporal, spatial, temporal and material meaning, Voz Pública is a set of interwoven dynamics and collaborative practices/production that immerse us in the stories of people and power while embroidering collective resistance.

#278 Ergon/Logos

By Paolo Pedercini (Molleindustria)

EDITORIAL:

Originally a work of flash poetry, Ergon/Logos has been updated for the post-Flash digital world as Windows/OSX standalone applications. It is a kinetic mix of poetry and branching storytelling, simply yet beautifully rendered in a horizontal scroll of white-on-black text. The frantic soundtrack reflects the hurried pace of the poem as it rushes by; the verse frequently branches, and the reader/player must quickly tap the spacebar to alter the flow down one track or another. The interactivity offers a material metaphor for the alternating angst and bravado conveyed in the textual content, an inner-versus-outer conflict that resonates with so many as they struggle with a sense of their own identity in opposition to prevailing cultural norms. LGBTQIA+ themes.

#279 aimisola.net/hymiwo.po

By Álvaro Seiça

EDITORIAL:

HYMIWO.PO (HYmn to imMIgrant WOmen, a Poem) explores the condition of African immigrant women living in Spain, from their point-of-view. The authors, European males, acknowledge that they don’t have firsthand experience either as Africans or as women. They’ve created a poetic structure that creates an interactive and playable experience. They also developed a wiki to host "a digital archive of audio, video and image” assembled by a Spanish NGO [non-governmental organization] that includes “interviews with immigrant women who live in Spain, language-learning and professional workshops, and social gatherings all designed to foster integration and psychosocial care.” In creating a playable experience of immigration, where “silence” can be moved by the player/reader but not accelerated in this side-scrolling display, the authors do not provide a beautiful interface. The piece’s calm music and slow pace disrupt any effort to “level up” and get to the next screen, as side-scrollers typically do. Instead, this poem-game provides an experience of living with the women’s words, which fade in and out of view, as the player (in the character of the word “silence”) slowly moves from left to right and out of view. The final screen “Poem Over” is a rich cerulean blue.

#282 Subcutanean

By Aaron A. Reed

EDITORIAL:

Subcutanean represents the conversion of several practices and genres of electronic and print literature. Reed terms his method “quantum authoring”: the work has a master hypertext of a branching narrative, and when a book is ordered/requested the “Subcutanean generator” (written in Python) collapses all the choices into one linear narrative. The result is a book with thousands of possible permutations, and you never know what you’re going to get. The story is a queer coming-of-age meets House of Leaves, as the protagonist explores a mysterious labyrinthine space of fear and uncertainty; on its own, in any permutation, it holds together in a fine text of eldritch horror for the new millennium. The work is also notable for its path to readers: originally offered as an IndieGoGo campaign, backers could opt to receive one permutation, or all 10,000 of them (delivered on a USB drive), along with the master text and the source code for the generator. As part of the campaign, Reed also created a pair of Twitter bots to tweet two permutations in parallel (@subcutanean2160 and @subcutanean6621), as well as versions for audiobook, Wattpad, Tapas, and Royal Road. This proliferation across mainstream platforms with a text that is both deeply co-authored by human and machine yet absolutely accessible to the wider reading public places Subcutanean in territory that few works of elit have attempted, in trying to break into book publishing as opposed to games distributors. For that, along with the sheer artistry of the narrative and the code, Subcutanean serves as a quintessential work of this particular era of elit.

#284 The Under Presents

By Samantha Gorman, Others (Tender Claws)

EDITORIAL:

The Under Presents delivers on a notion first hatched in 1991 by Brenda Laurel in her human-computer interface experiments at the Atari Corporation, documented in her book Computers as Theater. The Under Presents takes place in a sprawling absurdist world, but its home base is a nightclub-like space in the hull of a hulking overturned ship, where whimsical stage acts perform (often played by live actors in VR). The “Under” is an overturned hull of a sunken ship that becomes the playable space where guests wander, engage with live actors, and watch vaudeville-style stage performances by, for example, a green-skinned lounge performer flanked by her drumming skeleton sidekick. Journalist Joan E. Solsman notes that when The Under Presents (TUP) was in early development in 2018, Yelena Rachitsky, executive producer of experiences at Oculus, described it as a blend of indie video game Journey and the interactive theatrical experience Sleep No More, where the audience travels room-to-room in a spooky house, following characters from Macbeth. In TUP, you play a "sprite" that looks similar to the avatars in Journey. As you explore this fantasy world, you come in contact with other players and communicate wordlessly, through pantomime and finger snaps—as in Journey. TUP is replayable and, because of the live actors, would be different every time. It's meant to have a roughly three-hour story arc. Like Sleep No More, the player/audience member puts on a mask when entering this fantasy world. TUP uses the affordance of VR, allowing the audience to explore everything around them or follow paths led by crisscrossing live actors. The interplay of ten people on a ship on display in a bottle is TUP’s story-within-a-story. You unravel their backstory and their fate by scrubbing backward and forward through time and virtually following specific characters.

#368 The 24-Hour Micro elit Project

By Dene Grigar

EDITORIAL:

This early experimentation with elit microfiction (2009) highlights participatory co-authoring (pre-netprov) and serves as a bit of field archaeology. The 24-Hr. Micro-Elit Project explores flash fiction (i.e. the “short short story”) –a genre whose hallmark is extreme brevity while establishing both compelling character and complex plot development. Microstories or tiny tales have been around for some time, although the 24-Hr. Micro-Elit Project moved this tradition onto the internet in early days, creating an open and networked writing community with crowdsourced participation. The project produced a collection of twenty four stories about life in an American city in the twenty first century, along with a blog compendium of over eighty five stories submitted by more than twenty five participants from five countries. Each tiny tale was shaped by the Twitter constraint of 140 characters or less, delivered (or tweeted) on the social media platform over a twenty four hour period. Today, this approach is commonly known as twitterature, marked by the current 280-character constraint imposed by the medium (upgraded from 140 characters in late 2017) and spawning many new participatory fiction projects including interactive “twovels”.

#373 Minicontos Coloridos

By Marcelo Spalding

EDITORIAL:

Minicontos Coloridos [Colored short stories] is a series of mini-stories originally based on and inspired by colors, represented as gradations in the RGB [Red, Green, Blue] scale. This work explores the expressive possibilities of the medium in order to enhance the readers’ involvement with reading and writing, and how these can be affected by visual and color conventions deriving from painting. The website design is simple enough to achieve the goals, and the action required is straightforward: to choose a percentage of RGB. Subsequently, a short story related to that color is picked from the database. Although simple, the project is a remarkable pedagogical tool targeting younger audiences. It also involves a participatory dimension, contributing to expand language awareness and literacy with(in) digital media. To this point 34 authors have participated, including teachers, students and writers, in an open, evolving “work”. These microstories can be further related to the specific Latin-American context of “microcontos” (micro-tales, also known as nanocontos [nano-tales] or “microrrelatos” [micro-reports]), a literary form adopted by a considerable number of writers. Based on conciseness, precision, openness and fragmentation, it is easily adapted into eliterature. Although these stories are neither bots nor computer-generated, they establish the setting for the development of a ‘kids elit’, anticipating other short forms of production such as short text messaging, tweets and clips, Memes and animated GIFs.

#375 Seasonal Labyrinths

By Maurem Kayna

EDITORIAL:

Seasonal Labyrinths is a narrative experience that allows readers to assemble micro stories as they traverse between the four seasons. The reader can choose any starting point, any intermediate step, and any end season. The text fragments are microfictions, a literary form important in Latin America generally and Brazil particularly, the country in which Seasonal Labyrinths was created. In this cultural context, microfictions are concrete, concise and open, allowing people to recombine the microfictions into new stories. This playful tradition is easily adapted into recombinant eliterature. In Seasonal Labyrinths, the text is layered on top of photographs of seasonal images and presented in plain text. The reader may also choose to blindly travel through a simulated labyrinth, which would traverse one of the 64 possible combinations. In its original form, the reader could share the microfictions they create via social networks such as Facebook. That option is no longer available, but Seasonal Labyrinths was released as a printed book, with an ePUB version available for download.

#382 Upgrade Soul

By Eric Loyer, Ezra Claytan Daniels, Alexis Gideon

EDITORIAL:

Upgrade Soul is an interactive science fiction graphic novel that began as an app for iPhone and iPad (2012; completed 2019). Distributed serially chapter-by-chapter in 2012, the story went on a seven-year hiatus when developer Erik Loyer paused the project during a time when the Apple app store was an unstable environment in which to distribute literature. In the interim, Upgrade Soul story writer and illustrator Ezra Claytan Daniels pursued printed publication with Lion Forge, which published the graphic novel in 2018. Both the app and printed versions were met with great acclaim. In 2019, Loyer made the first chapter of Upgrade Soul freely available on iPad and iPhone, though the Apple publishing environment remains unstable because the App store typically purges works that haven’t been updated for 24 months—even if they don’t need updating. The story follows an elderly couple (Molly’s a scientist; Hank’s a wealthy science aficionado) determined to de-age themselves via a process called “Upgrade Cell.” The experiment goes haywire. Molly and Hank survive, but are confronted with disaster: utterly disfigured but intellectually and physically superior duplicates of themselves. Several other characters, including the ambitious and misguided geneticist who performs the experiment, enrich this fascinating story. Also notable: none of the main characters is racially white. Loyer’s interactive 3D and dynamic soundscape enhance the horror and psychological tension. Interactive elements convey depth of human interconnection that printed text can’t do, such as the 3D telescoping effect as a reader physically senses a character’s epiphany. Loyer’s long experience making deep, emotionally satisfying work through touch screen interactivity and sound finds an apex in Upgrade Soul.

#383 Kentucky Route Zero

By Jake Elliott, Tamas Kemenczy, Ben Babbit

EDITORIAL:

A walking simulator that unfolded in five acts released 2013-2020, Kentucky Route Zero is about meeting people in strange places, lingering with them, and letting their stories guide reveal a core truth about alienation from the American Dream. Playing as Conway, a delivery guy and drifter, the player is ostensibly on a job to deliver an antique, but the route becomes surreal: the basement of an empty gas station; a decommissioned and haunted mine where a flood killed the family members of your companion, Shannon; a cathedral; a museum of suburban houses. Conversations with NPCs [non-player characters] are consequential, allowing the gamer to decide through their conversational choices whether a person is over a former lover, or has recovered from a life-changing event. Most of the story is told through character dialogue and exploration. Set in rural America, people hard hit by globalization and impoverished by forces beyond their control, Kentucky Route Zero creates playable experiences where those forces intersect with interpersonal relationships. If a game is a “series of interesting choices,” as Sid Meyer said, then Kentucky Route Zero sets those choices in a seven-years-in-the-making episodic drama of American loss, a gothic landscape where the eerie seems like a reasonable reaction to awe and disempowerment.

#384 c-ya-laterrrr

By Dan Hett

EDITORIAL:

c-ya-laterrrr is a deeply emotional autobiographical Twine game conveying the experiences of the author on 22 May 2017 and the days that followed: the day of the bombing at an Ariana Grande concert at Manchester Arena in Manchester, England. The prose is heartbreakingly written, demonstrating how the power of language persists in interactive media. Presented as black text in lexias centered on a white background, the work is stripped back entirely in order to place ultimate emphasis on the language; it is not the default style for Twine games, but rather a deliberate design choice that privileges written narrative in a multimodal space. The branching narrative explores the “would have/could have/should have” of experiencing trauma and loss: the unknowns, the phone calls, the visits, the conversations with family and friends, and how choices filter through the memories of traumatic events. This text in particular demonstrates that creating highly affective elit doesn’t have to be about flashy digital tricks and algorithms; rather, it shows maturity in the use of its medium for the greatest impact on its audience.

#385 The Book You Are Looking For Does Not Exist

By Vera Sebert

EDITORIAL:

The Book You Are Looking For Does Not Exist is an interactive webzine in six vignettes that stage writing, reading and listening as performances. The reader must discover the text through audio and touch feedback. Vignettes one and two are asemic writing, that which almost makes sense, but doesn’t resolve into patterns we can discern as words. Vignette three shines a spotlight on an otherwise blacked-out text; to read it, one hovers using touchpad to point the spotlight and discover the aphorism. Vignette four is a scene of disfigurement, where to engage with the text via touchpad is to make it less legible. Vignette five, “cannibal code” ventures forth into the other vignettes. Vignette six is a “lesson in improving your English,” discovered via a cursor shaped like a pen one draws across the blank canvas, triggering words that sound like gibberish until one figures out the right pace to hear sensible words. The “book” made by Vera Sebert unfolds into performative acts.

#388 Travesty Generator

By Lillian-Yvonne Bertam

EDITORIAL:

Lillian-Yvonne Bertram’s Travesty Generator is both ironic and deeply felt. The book’s metaphor of systemic racism as encoded—predictable, logical, pattern-making—is to suggest that white supremacy and murder of Black people is so baked into American culture as to be its operating system. And yet there’s no distance here, no ironic vantage, on “Three Last Words,” a Python script that outputs variants of Eric Garner’s dying words as he was being choked to death by an off duty police officer: “I can’t breathe.” Bertram comments the code: “#return” “#this articulation” “#the exhaustion” #we can’t stop hearing.” Reading this first poem in Bertram’s collection gives a jolt of recognition, the slamming together of horror and the banal repeatability of code. It can, and does, run again, and again, and again. The second poem, “Coming of Age Stories,” lists precautions Black parents instruct their children to take, things to do in emergencies and in circumstances that are ordinary and unavoidable. Bertram’s deft work in these poems and the entire collection (available at Noemi Press) uses algorithms to tell intimate stories about Trayvon Martin, Harriet Tubman, Emmett and Mamie Till—and all of us who recognize this history as a travesty generator.

FIN

#389 80 Days

By InkleStudios/Emily Morganti

EDITORIAL:

In 2014, 80 Days was voted best novel of the year (The Telegraph) and one of the top ten best games of the year (Time magazine). Based on Jules Verne’s Around the World in 80 Days, this text-based game brilliantly adapts the original novella’s core mechanic: a race against the clock to find a route circumventing the world and return to London. As Passepartout, valet to Phineas Fogg (who wagers a fortune on his speedy traversal), the player encounters a huge range of characters set in various locales who can increase Fogg’s health, strength or wealth. Steampunk in style, 80 Days includes a range of invented vehicles and gadgets even as it deals authentically with social realities glossed over in Jules Verne’s source text: racial bias; the legacy of colonialism; gender fluidity; homophilia. 80 Days is a blast to play, and the reader/player is hard-pressed to choose between beating the clock and delving into fascinating conversation with NPCs. It is commercially available.

FIN

#390 All Your Time-Tossed Selves

By Porpentine

EDITORIAL:

Porpentine is known for nothing if not playing with digital media, from Twine games to ebooks. With All Your Time-Tossed Selves, she has innovated with a rather ubiquitous and unexpected medium: Google Forms. With options for radio buttons, drop-down lists, multiple choice, and new section reveals, Google Forms is a surprising yet effective option for a work of poetic narrative such as this one. Set in the ruins of a dying city, the work presents as line and verse, with the reader/player choosing which to keep, which to play. While the options are limited and the narrative necessarily fairly linear, given the constraints of the (literal) form, Porpentine molds the medium to the work, offering a very strong illusion of choice that nonetheless winds its way through rubble to construct an affective tale. It’s short—only a 2-5 minute playthrough—which encourages replay and multiplicative experiences, and the use of Forms affords one fascinating element: the ability to view the data of all the playthroughs, the previous responses to the work. It adds another layer to the environment of destruction, as your experience is solitary, and yet you can view the trails of other readers/players writ on the work itself.

#391 The River Poem

By Jeneen Naji

EDITORIAL:

The River Poem is an intersection between place, history, heritage, poetry, and artificial intelligence. It is an installation piece, as the text is projected onto a 3D model of Dublin City, the poetic verses flowing along the River Liffey. Dublin’s heritage is rich with literature, as the writers Kate O’Brien, James Joyce, Augusta Gregory, Jonathan Swift, Elizabeth Bowen, Oscar Wilde, and many many others all called it home at one time or another. The River Poem calls on that heritage, using Joyce’s Finnegans Wake as the training text for the AI’s learning algorithm, processing the work and generating the poetic verses from its prose. The result is an apt, unending stream of cyborg Irish poetry in the center of a pristine miniature of the city, a mix of new technology in a bed of long-established history, lit with the words that heralded a paradigmatic change in literature.

By Gwenyth Nava

EDITORIAL:

"We are body" enables a different thought than "we have a body," says Gwenyth Nava, a GenZ new media artist from Mexico City exploring the contiguities between words and the physical body that speaks or writes them. #395 EXPOSED

By Sharon Daniel & Erik Loyer

EDITORIAL:

Two million people are incarcerated in the U.S. prison system, a disproportionately high number of them Black and brown people. On March 21, 2020, the first case of a prisoner infected with Coronavirus was reported in Brooklyn, New York, followed two days later by the first case in California’s vast prison system. EXPOSED is a database and interactive timeline that gathers hundreds of audio testimonies from prisoners and their family members in addition to quotes and statistics collected from a comprehensive array of online publications and broadcasts. Any day during the Coronavirus offers abundant testimony to the risk and trauma that prisoners experienced under coronavirus quarantine. On July 8, 2020 alone, there are over 100 statements by prisoners afflicted with the virus or enduring anxiety, distress, and severe hardship. Family members report lack of access to information, such as talking with their incarcerated relative one day and a few days later, being called in by prison officials to identify the body. This work of eliterature uses the affordances of a database and a stylish, monochromatic user interface to make this epic story scalable. The reader’s freedom and choice to sample the materials—using date, headline, or first words of a testimony—is juxtaposed against the increasingly harsh restrictions placed on prisoners during the deadly, seemingly limitless quarantine.

#399 Masked Making

By Lai-Tze Fan, Anastasia Salter, Anne Sullivan

EDITORIAL:

When the world went into lockdown to prevent the spread of COVID-19 in 2020, masks were in short supply, reserved for medical professionals and other Essential Workers. Masked Making, authored by three women artist/scholars during the lockdown period, documents the vast, distributed and largely invisible collective of women’s craft labor: those who sewed cloth masks for family, neighbors, and others in their communities. Masked Making, a generative poem, endlessly cycles through imagetexts, making public this work largely undertaken in private spaces and shared in personal social media accounts. Collected news items, social media images, and personal reflections are gathered by the authors “to represent the wealth of diversity, age groups, and communities that participated in collective mask making.” The simple, direct testimonies of the fictional-but-representative women instantly conjures the emotions of lockdown: the longing for a return to social contact and the ethical commitment to keep people safe from the virus even during mask scarcity. Eventually in the U.S., the mask became to large swaths of the population a politicized symbol of infringement on personal liberty. This generative work recalls the earlier moments in lockdown, when the donated supplies and labor of these skilled crafters evoked unity against a deadly, worldwide virus.

#400 Blackout Poetry Tool

By Jazer Chand

EDITORIAL:

Blackout poetry modifies an existing text by “blacking out” some words in the passage; the remaining words are read as a poem. Student Jazer Chand made the Blackout Poetry Tool as a way of exploring binary systems and thinking: visible/invisible, knowable/unknowable, and the “human/computer dichotomy” that can be traced to Aristotle and the philosophy of binary thinking. (See his cogent explication of “Blackout Poetry Tool In the Context of Human/Computer Dichotomy” linked off the work’s main page.) There are four modes of play (you choose the words that are not blacked out; a bot chooses; a combination of you and the bot choose; you choose and the bot suggests, which is a lot of fun). A fifth option, the bot draws a wave, is an inventive twist on the blackout poetry genre. Blackout poetry rewards strategic forethought, akin to lace where the delicate gaps between stitches convey the lace’s beauty. But it can be just as fun to run Blackout Poetry Tool speedthroughs, randomly and quickly clicking. Chand has chosen Frankenstein as the source text: a lovely intertextual choice signaling the dichotomy between creator and “monster.” Chand summons Mary Shelley’s irony: it is cold Frankenstein, not the soulful Creature, who betrays humane impulses–suggesting that the human/computer “dichotomy” is hardly absolute.

#401 Meghadūtam

By Priti Pandurangan

EDITORIAL:

“Cloud messengers” are a trope of ancient Sanskrit poetry by Kālādasā (5th century CE). An estranged lover, separated from the beloved, looks for something to alleviate melancholy, and ideally deliver a message to the estranged lover. In Priti Pandurangan’s fluid, kinetic typography, layers of significance emanate from multiple acts of translation. The poem snippets she reads are nineteenth-century British translations of the ancient Sanskrit; Pandurangan’s gorgeously minimal, kinetic typography uses the Latin alphabet (the most widely used alphabet in the world) to translate the Sanskrit into modern words contemporary Indians could read. And then there is the birdsong and ocean waves soundscapes, further emplacing the reader in Pandurangan’s naturalistic setting of these word sculptures rendered from ancient texts. The result is multimodal: rhymed, iambic reading rolling in time with the waves, while the reader uses arrow keys to gain perspective on the 3D words.

#402 Leaning Haiku

EDITORIAL:

“The nod is a poetry in itself.” Using what he calls the “infamous Indian nod,” as the key mechanic in his haiku generator, Praveen Sinha built an Instagram AR filter that reads your nod which triggers lines of a haiku based on the direction of your nod. A left nod generates “sad vibes”; a right nod generates “joy/love vibes.” The result is an amusing set of haikus that hover above your head as you nod. While haiku generators abound on the web, Sinha’s distinctively appropriates a cultural commonplace—the nod—for a humorous, intimate engagement. “Her Head leaned / Once Left, Once Right / We were married.” The nod “can be used for anything actually,” Sinha notes, “yes, no, don't know, all good, not good, etc.” Such broad gestural meaning of the nod maps well onto the arrays Sinha built (line one: observations from nature; line two: evocation from human emotions; line 3: a philosophical truth.) It’s a fascinating use of Instagram filters for a culturally rich and funny update of the ancient haiku.

#409 Lagos At Large

By Jumoke Sanwo

EDITORIAL:

What does it mean to come home? In this “uneasy love story,” Jumoke Sanwo makes an ode to Lagos, the largest city in Nigeria. We are immersed in the busy-ness of Lagos, always on the go: at a bus station where one is immersed in “hustling,” at markets, inside a bus, and at the posh lagoon where one can nibble “vegan, gluten-free” treats and do yoga against the gorgeous backdrop of the lagoon. Part memoir, part travelogue, Lagos-At-Large is told through the voice of Njideka, an Austrian/Nigerian spoken word artist contemplating a return home. Legacies of colonialism and present-day economic exploitation from offshore investors are interwoven with the human cost of generational loss: “depression” caused by thinking too much—though Njideka assures us the pace of just getting by in Lagos moves fast there’s no time for depressive rumination. Told in collages and montages, Lagos-At-Large immerses us in one slice of the African diaspora: the bittersweet longing for a home with a long history of being compromised by forces beyond local control.
