#410 The Vine and the Fish

By Leise Hook

EDITORIAL:

An interactive webcomic originally published in The Believer (Oct. 2020, “The Survival Issue”), The Vine and the Fish is an autobiography about an Asian-American middle schooler who moves from Michigan to central Virginia--“the south,” as the narrator tells us with trepidation. “Other Asian families were few and far between.” The wash of pale green over the pen-and-ink style drawing is a chromatic reference to the kudzu vine: “an invasive, non-native species in the U.S.” Initially, the kudzu vine was hailed as a cure for soil erosion and a beautiful plant with aromatic leaves. But once it became known as “the vine that ate the south,” the point-of-view shifted, and kudzu was blamed for eroding fish, wildlife, and “decreasing property values.” Leise Hook’s extended metaphor of the kudzu and the “invasive” Asian carp are juxtaposed against President Trump calling Coronavirus the “Chinese” virus, and his subsequent declaration that the gesture “isn’t racist at all.” Author Hook uses the racist fears of fish and vines to ask: can we understand the ecosystem, or each other, if we frame them through language of invasion and danger? Hook’s interactive webcomic situates these large questions on an individual scale, a displaced teenager–a fish out of water–finding her way in a new home.

#411 Le Lac

By Nyasha Kandanara

EDITORIAL:

Le Lac is an immersive, VR experience told from the point-of-view of Lake Chad, a large freshwater lake in West Africa that 45 million people depend upon. The VR experience shows a day in the life of the Lake, focusing on a nomadic farmer and a fisherman, who is now also a refugee due to Boko Haram insurgency. Because Lake Chad has lost 90% of its former surface area, “she” has less to give the inhabitants who rely on her. Filmmaker Nyasha Kandandara depicts Lake Chad as a nonhuman agent in the region, a benevolent maternal entity who feels “complete helplessness.” Wondering if my shores will swell and spill over as they did decades ago.” Kandandara began this project because she wondered: “How does one go from being a vast body of water to scattered ponds?” With skill and compassion, Kandandara puts viewers right in the action of the Lake, and one feels the urgency of the shrinking surface area and the ever-present threat of the “black flags” of Boko Haram. “It's not just the black flags that worry me,” says the Lake. “I am not who I used to be.”

#412 Writer's Tools™

By Milton Läufer

EDITORIAL:

This collection of 10 WriterTools™ allows users to visualize, manipulate and transform texts. Programmed by Läufer between 2014 and 2019, it provides interesting clues about what constitutes translation and transcoding in digital media, in an elegant and intelligible manner. These tools also compel us to address the (often artificially) constructed borderline separating digital humanities (dh) and electronic literature (elit). Composing a coherent set of ‘mechanisms’ that entice readers to engage with texts and within textuality, they imply a creative engagement with language (elit), as well as constitute adequate means for textual analysis (dh); they allow users to play with existing or new text, changing parameters and variables, hence playing the role of a computer assistant (dh) and/or a generative and interactive creative partner (elit). The different operations supported by the WriterTools™ grant similar ample perspectives: translating text to sound; representing connections between corpora of texts; creating visual and interactive representations of texts; replacing words from the input text with images and/or texts dynamically collected from the Internet, etc. The WriterTools™ are ironic about the belief of Genius and as such in addition to asking “Do Bots Worry About Writer's Block?” maybe one could as well respond that with these sophisticated tools, resulting from an expressive dialog between human creator and algorithms, Writers Should Not Worry About Bots.

#413 Legends of Michigami

By M.D. Coverley

EDITORIAL:

A poet of the west and western landscapes, M.D. Coverley is a pioneer of electronic literature. Her multimodal hypertext work Califia (2000), a delicious wander through nineteenth-century California, featured songs given to her by the Grateful Dead. Initially drawn to make eliterature in the 1990s because she wanted to use color and hypertextual sequencing to tell stories, thirty years later Coverley’s Prairie Chants and Riding the Rust Belt traverse western landscapes through video shot from windows of Amtrak trains. She superimposes contemporary images of former prairielands (such as present-day Chicago) with historical images, Indigenous prairie tribal letters, and poetry. Legends of Michigami comment on environmental degradation and the violent removal of Native peoples from their land. These later works tell a story also of how a pioneer like Coverley makes work with off-the-shelf, simple-to-use technologies. Taken in the context of her long career, these short multimodal works focalize some of her abiding and important themes: how families are rooted in the land; how perspectives on relationships and “paths taken” shift as we age.

#414 Immersive Poetry

By Jose Aburto

EDITORIAL:

Immersive Poetry by Jose Aburto combines three 3D poems published on Facebook (2016) and one filter posted on Instagram (2021, currently available in Facebook, both subsidiaries of Meta Platforms). They were crafted using Spark VR, and can be fully adventured using VR hardware or as an alternative a simple mobile phone or web browser will do the work. The 3D poems are surrounding texts (“Disolvencias [Dissolvences]” and “Condensaciones [Condensations]”) that elude their readers by spinning and turning, finally returning to their initial point of departure. Confined in this loop and thus trapped on a web, readers are presented successive expressions of grief (“en refugio en sombra en encierro (...) en temor [in refuge in shadow in confinement (...) in fear])”; and the spherical poem “Volver [To Return]”, synthesizing the previous whirling, is a 3D sphere with forking paths, for readers to wander “una y otra vez hasta encontrar el límite [over and over again until finding the limit]”. The experiment with filter technology (“Somos Máscaras [We Are Masks]”) simulates writing on the users’ face. The word “Somos [We Are]” is displayed over the face, in changing colors, and upon opening the mouth, the word “Máscaras [Masks]” materializes, coming out of and dancing around the mouth. This suggests that in an hypermediated society we are all masks alike, regardless of our differences. The real masks and filters are inside us, they are not external. Aburto experimented a variety of medial approaches to poetry: from concrete/visual to electronic forms, from printed matter to sculpture. The fact that “Volver [To Return]” was also printed as a ‘real’ 3D sphere further articulates his concerns with remediation. These lucid poems are speculative and critical about the platforms where they engage, using their technological characteristics to produce an unusual product that delivers unconventional results, concentrating on content and thus reaching a level of literary value where language and identity play significant roles.

#415 Ciberpoesia

By Michael Hurtado Enríquez

EDITORIAL:

Ciberpoesia [Cyberpoetry] includes seven creative experiments with code and language by Hurtado Enríquez. Manifestly simple, yet efficient and genuine, these works adopt a universal language (JavaScript) but nonetheless focus on a specific language (Spanish) and a particular cultural identity (Peruvian). Poetic texts are presented as a starting point for interaction and simultaneously act as a tool to motivate readers to become writers. The premise is uncomplicated and the interface is clear-cut: a manipulable short poem inside a text area; buttons to “enviar [send]” and “borra [restart]”; formatting options (font, color, size); a blank screen to play with the text after “enviar [send]” is triggered. This canvas (element and interface) is the central stage for interaction, i.e., for reading-writing-reading: it “alberga todas las posibilidades que hay en el universo [houses all the possibilities in the universe].” As users click and drag their mouse or finger in and around this blank surface, they paint with words/sentences in the text area. Texts shift, move and bounce in planographic or three-dimensional space, isolated or combined with other texts. Furthermore, the transformations in the text embed some properties of the input texts, motivating users to write new input texts to establish analogous relations with the described operations. Some cyberpoems do not allow readers to change the source text, but they relate to others in honoring Peruvian experimental poetry. Cyberpoem #6, for instance, adapts a literary text from the Peruvian repertoire to include numbers and emojis. Five vowels fly around the mouse cursor, activating a visual poem by Javier Sologuren (“Viento de vocales [Wind from vowels]”, 1977). Reverberating the experimental tradition in visual and phonic resources, these works demonstrate why Lit(e)Lat (Literatura Electrónica Latinoamericana) is such a strong and vibrant elit community.
